en: Preface to the *Dharmapada-sūtra-dhāraṇī-pratyaya-ji*:

The *Lotus Sūtra* is the king among all sūtras. With his broad and long tongue, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime cause of the "Plucking of the Flower," synthesizing the secret essentials of all dharmas.
He revealed the provisional to manifest the real, unifying the three vehicles into one perfect vehicle. Comprising seven fascicles in total, it contains approximately sixty thousand [verses].
It is said: "How vast and flowing! This is truly a great vision. Nevertheless, on that day at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Buddha preached a distinct teaching during each of the five periods:
first the *Avataṃsaka*, second the *Āgama*, third the *Vaipulya*, and fourth the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Yet, even then, he felt his intent was not yet fully expressed;
thus, at the very end, he again preached this sutra to transform immeasurable and boundless Dharma-bodies and to expound immeasurable [truths].
The mouth of the Dharma of boundlessness is overflowing with inversion; one need not regret prolixity of words. Is this not already much for the World-Honored One?
Formerly, when the Buddha was approaching nirvana, Mañjuśrī requested that the Buddha turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. The Buddha rebuked him, saying:
"I have dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, yet I have never spoken a single word. Your request for me to turn the wheel of the Dharma again implies that I have already turned it."
Is it the Wheel of Dharma? Indeed, a single word was not spoken; he sat facing the wall for nine years.
Since he already sat facing the wall for nine years, as for this one word—why even need it be spoken?
If one can skillfully awaken to these sixty thousand or so words, then one may break those sixty thousand words into a single word, and further, one may break that single word back into wordlessness.
Furthermore, how could it be impossible for the unspoken to expand into sixty thousand words?

And how could it be impossible for those sixty thousand words to be transformed into hundreds of billions of words? Once knowledge and vision are opened, the perfect teaching is suddenly and completely penetrated. Such is the wondrous Dharma.

"Is it much? It is not much. Now, within these myriad worlds—a weary house on fire—having fortunately been invited by the universal illumination of the white light, we have been granted the opportunity to receive this sutra.
Truly, it is a bridge across the path of birth and death, and a flight of stairs to the gate of the Pure Land.
As stated in the sutra, there is an earnest entrustment regarding the bestowal of predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); as for its subsequent transmission...
The Dharma has, roughly speaking, five gates. The most supreme is upholding it; next are explaining, reciting, copying, and making offerings of it.

Even if it be but a single phrase or a single verse, should one vow to take refuge in it, then regardless of whether they be a rustic villager, a son within the inner chambers, a prisoner or one afflicted by chronic illness, or even among the scales and feathers of the animal kingdom—indeed, for all sentient beings possessed of blood and breath—[the merit is immeasurable].
We are all devoted with sincerity and together partake in the compassionate rain.

How much more so for one who upholds the tradition of the Great Awakened One and elucidates the profound meaning of Kāśyapa’s teachings—truly what is called a "Guide, an Elephant among Men," and a "Dry City" within the Dharma-realm?
Now, as for the lotus flower, it is valued because it emerges from the mud yet remains unstained. The dust and fire-houses of the five turbidities are far more than mere mud; yet seeking therein...
This stands alone as unstained; were it not for hearing the wondrous Dharma, there would be no way to liberation.
Thus we know that on that day, the World-Honored One intended, by means of this sutra’s name, to take the entire land of Zhendan and plant within it but a single blue lotus.
Seeking the stem through the flower, and seeking the root through the stem—whether compared to the autumn pond of the Jade Well or the Flower-Pool of the Virtuous Water—is this one or two?
Please look from this precious throne situated between the three periods of time. If the thousand layers are manifest right before one’s eyes, where else would one seek the *utpala*?

It is not separate from form and fragrance; it clearly demonstrates cause and effect. How could this deceive me? How could this deceive me? Having completed the compilation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

Accounts of Its Practice and Verification, I reflect that this sutra is a profound ocean of the Buddha’s teachings, and its widespread propagation is a matter of urgency. Thus, moved by [this realization]...

These accounts of spiritual wonders have been recorded in successive compilations. Accordingly, I have selected verified accounts of the deeds and experiences of virtuous sages and ancient masters from successive dynasties that are sufficient to inspire conviction.
Following the format of previous collections, I have organized them here; it is my hope that those who see or hear of them will apply themselves with diligence to cultivation and practice.
They equally realize samādhi. From the teaching that the three are one, there emerges the ultimate, subtle principle that nothing can be said.

The verse of Caoqi says: "When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the Lotus Sutra; when the mind is awakened, it turns the Lotus Sutra. To understand this is to realize that the appearance of this sutra is for the sake of the great cause and condition.
The true awakening of the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemn and vivid through the ages. My own words—how much more so!
Ah! Written by Zhou Kefu,
a disciple of the Pure Practice [Society] in Yangxian, after fasting and bathing,
as a preface to encourage the circulation of the *Dhāraṇī for the Retention of the Lotus Sūtra* and its verified accounts of efficacy.
Wherever the scriptures are located, their circulation constitutes a virtuous condition (*kuśala-pratyaya*), and the resulting merit and retribution are immeasurable. Thus it is said:

"One who can transmit the Mahāyāna Dharma to a single person shall receive the merit of ten good deeds; one who transmits it to ten people shall receive the merit of a hundred good deeds; and one who transmits it to a person of great status [shall receive even greater merit]."
Those who are great heroes and possess great power shall receive a thousand merits; those who reprint and widely disseminate this work shall receive ten thousand merits.
How much more so for the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, which transcends the cycle of birth and death, never regresses, and continues until the attainment of Buddhahood.
This exhortation for a single person to cultivate the Pure Land is precisely the means by which one brings a sentient being to the realization of Buddhahood.
All who attain Buddhahood must necessarily deliver immeasurable sentient beings; those beings whom they deliver all originate with me.
Therefore, the karmic reward of this merit is truly inexhaustible. For this reason, I wish to exhort all who see and hear this to broaden their minds through the Buddha.

Take this mind as your own mind; cause every person to know it so that they may all be reborn in the Pure Land. As for what Longshu has said, one should naturally believe it with earnest conviction, for it is not false.
As for the two sutras of the *Lotus* and the *Avataṃsaka*, they are especially the most supreme vehicle (*yāna*) among the wondrous teachings spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who universally delivers the world and manifests in every land, the accounts of how past worthies were moved and attained communion with him are recorded throughout history.

All these matters are clearly manifest. I have compiled them individually to encourage the cultivation of practice. This is truly the most expedient gateway for those yet to come, serving as a bell and chime to awaken them and a bridge and raft for those on the final path.
In the autumn of the Wuxu year, I compiled the *Records of Experiences in Holding the Vajra*, for which I have already written a brief preface for circulation.
I now respectfully entreat my fellow practitioners to publish these records of experiences in holding the names of Amitābha, the Lotus Sūtra, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and Avalokiteśvara.

I have searched through the archives and collected records, verifying the accounts from both ancient and modern times. I have exerted considerable effort of mind and hand, intending to dedicate my devotion to this imperishable work.
However, as the blocks for printing were produced here, they have not yet been widely disseminated to other provinces.

Since we all dwell together within the adorned Buddha-land, how could we allow for a deficiency in the excellence of the circulation of the Dharma? I therefore appeal once more to the faithful of the present age who may obtain [this text].
Having examined various editions, I have not been parsimonious in carving them for wide distribution.

Whether following the original texts or revising this compilation, I hope that all those who come across these works and possess accounts of their own experiences or verifications will continue to add to them in the future. To offer praise for even a single phrase is to nurture the roots of virtue;
to stir the mind for even a single moment is to eliminate a lifetime of karmic offenses. By means of this, may the lineage continue.
The Buddha’s wisdom-life consists in benefiting both oneself and others. This refers to the various deities who protect the Dharma;

having protected the Jewel of the Dharma, they will certainly and without fail protect those who propagate the Dharma and carry its treasures. In the past, the sages drew the "Splitting the Nest" (Pike-ko) diagram to encourage people to recite the Buddha’s name.

Later, when others were reborn in the Pure Land due to their recitation, they attributed the merit to the person who had provided the diagram, and that person likewise attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
The merit of the Dharma-giving is inconceivable, such as this. I pray that you and all fellow practitioners will together exhort one another.
By the person who practices the Way of Goodness, Ke-fu, with utmost sincerity.

Shi Tanmola-che (translated into Chinese as Dharmarakṣa, "Dharma Protector") was from Dunhuang Commandery during the Jin dynasty. His original surname was Zhi.

He entered the monastic order at the age of eight and could recite ten thousand words of scripture daily. With the resolve to propagate the Great Way, he traveled extensively through the various kingdoms of the Western Regions and returned to China carrying Sanskrit scriptures.

He subsequently translated various sections, including the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin, he retired to live in seclusion in the deep mountains. In those mountains...
There was a clear stream from which he constantly took water for washing and rinsing. Later, it suddenly became defiled and dried up.

The Master paced back and forth, sighing, "Because people possess such meager virtue, this pure spring has ceased its flow. As soon as he finished speaking, the stream surged forth, filling the ravine. Such was the power of his profound sincerity;
at that time, he was renowned as the "Bodhisattva of Dunhuang."

Kumārajīva, whose name in the language of China means "Child Longevity," was a native of India. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and could recite a thousand verses daily. At twelve, he traveled to the kingdom of Kucha;
while engaged in preaching the Dharma, he devoted himself exclusively to the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) scriptures. Consequently, his reputation filled the region east of the Pamirs.
The King of Kucha welcomed him back to his own country and requested that he elucidate the profound mysteries of the Vaipulya sūtras. The Master then proceeded to analyze and expound upon them.

"All phenomena are empty and without self; the analysis of the aggregates and elements is merely a provisional designation and not real. Upon hearing this, there was no one who did not gain insight and awakening.

During the Fu Qin period, the Grand Historian reported that a star had appeared in the celestial sphere corresponding to foreign lands, signifying that a person of great wisdom would enter to assist the Middle Kingdom.

He immediately dispatched an envoy to seek him out. In the twelfth month of the third year of Hongshi during the Later Qin dynasty, he welcomed the Master to Chang’an, where he stayed at the Xiaoyao Garden.
There, he translated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; its meanings were perfectly comprehensive, and the assembly was deeply satisfied and submissive.

Subsequently, he produced translations of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, and various treatises, totaling more than three hundred fascicles. The Master had always been fond of the Mahāyāna.

His aspirations were vast and expansive. As he approached his end, he addressed the assembly, saying: "I pray that what I have translated and proclaimed may be widely disseminated by all in future generations.
Now, before this assembly, I make a sincere and truthful vow: if what I have transmitted is without error, may my tongue not be scorched or consumed after my self-immolation.
In the fifth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he passed away in Chang’an. He was cremated according to foreign rites; when the wood was exhausted, his body remained.
He underwent cremation, yet his tongue alone did not turn to ash.
During the Jin dynasty, the Indian bhikṣu Mahāra recited the Mahāyāna sūtras; his virtuous conduct became increasingly renowned, and the king’s faith was upright.
He constantly spread his hair to cover the mud so that others might tread upon it. At times he said to the King, "This man has not read many scriptures;
why provide such great offerings for him? The King replied, "Once at midnight, I wished to see this bhikṣu.
I went immediately to his location and saw him in a cave reciting the Lotus Sūtra. There was a person of golden radiance riding a white elephant king, who joined his palms [in reverence]."
I made offerings, but when I drew near, he was no longer to be seen. I therefore asked the bhikṣu, "Has this golden-colored person vanished because I arrived?
The bhikṣu replied, "This is the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. Samantabhadra himself said:

'If there is anyone who recites the Lotus Sūtra, I shall come riding upon a white elephant to instruct them. Because I read this sūtra, Samantabhadra came here of his own accord. Thus spoke Samantabhadra.
This is none other than Samantabhadra Bodhisattva mentioned in the sutra. Having heard this, I prostrated at his feet and withdrew.
Therefore, I shall now diligently make offerings.
Shi Badaocheng of Chang’an during the Jin dynasty left the household life at the age of twenty. His faculties were dull and slow, yet he vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra daily.
He recorded a single line or even half a verse. Thus, through diligent toil, it was only upon reaching the age of eighty that he finally mastered one entire section.
One day, he suddenly saw a divine being in vermilion robes holding a document that said, "The Heavenly Emperor respectfully invites the Great Virtuous One.

The Master replied, "Since my birth, I have recited and upheld [the scriptures], praying exclusively for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. Although the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is superior, it is not what I desire. Thereupon, the spirit took its leave. Again, one night...

He dreamed of a great stupa made of the seven precious gems, in which his own body resided on the fifth tier. From there, he gazed upon a city of the seven precious gems with stairways extending beyond all bounds.

Two *vajra*-wielding deities stood there holding maces, while dozens of attendants in blue robes held white fly-whisks and swept the stairway, saying, "This is the Precious City of the West, come to welcome Baoteng.
Upon waking from the dream, he immediately ordered that his robes and alms bowl be used to provide for the assembly.
[The Master] observed the fast. He asked, "Do you all see the thousand Buddhas at this moment? The assembly replied, "We do not see them. He asked again, "Do you perceive an extraordinary fragrance?
The assembly replied, "We all smell it. Having spoken these words, he passed away peacefully toward the west.
The Jin dynasty monk Shi Huiyuan was surnamed Jia and was a native of Yanmen. Having heard the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he attained a sudden and profound awakening.

He subsequently cast aside his hairpin to renounce secular life and receive instruction, dedicating himself to profound reflection and the recitation of the scriptures. In the sixth year of the Taiyuan era, he arrived at Mount Lu.
He resided at Longquan Jingśe (Dragon Spring Hermitage) and wished to establish an araṇya (monastery), yet he still lacked fine timber. Moved by this, a mountain deity appeared in a dream;
one night there was a great storm and thunder, and when dawn broke, wood was piled up like a forest.

The Regional Inspector, Huan Yi, marveled at this divine marvel and consequently established a monastery called Donglin (Eastern Grove), with its main hall named Shenyun (Divine Operation). The Master once remarked that while the names of the samādhis in the various teachings are numerous...

The assembly, recognizing that spiritual progress is easily achieved through high merit, took the practice of *nienfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) as their priority. Consequently, they formed a society for *nienfo* with Huiyong, Huichi, and others; these were popularly known as the "Eighteen Worthies.
Furthermore, he led a group of one hundred and twenty-three people to collectively cultivate the Pure Land practices.

Throughout the six periods of the day and night, they practiced meditation and recitation without ceasing. There was a Dharma Master named Huiyi, who was forceful, upright, and rarely pleased; he once came to the mountain and encountered [the assembly].
When the Master lectured on the Lotus Sūtra, whenever he wished to pose difficult questions, he would suddenly feel a trembling in his heart and break into a sweat.

He remarked, "This gentleman’s speech and demeanor are truly worthy of my reverence and submission. The monks of the Western Lands all proclaim that China possesses Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, and they constantly pay homage toward the East.
For over thirty years, the Master had set his will upon the West; having three times beheld sacred visions, he remained silent and did not speak of them. During the Yixi era...

On the evening of the last day of the seventh month in the twelfth year, while rising from meditative absorption in the eastern niche of the Prajñā Terrace, he beheld Amitābha Buddha, his body filling the void of space.
Within the halo of light were immeasurable transformation Buddhas, with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta standing in attendance to his left and right.
He further saw flowing water and radiant light divided into fourteen streams, swirling upward and downward, proclaiming the wondrous Dharma.
The Buddha said, "By the power of my original vow, I have come to comfort you. Seven days from now, you shall be reborn in my land.
He also saw Buddhabhadra, Huichi, Huoyong, and Liu Yimin standing by the Buddha's side; they stepped forward, bowed to the Master, and said:

The Master’s aspiration had been set upon this from the beginning. "Why have you arrived so late? he said. Knowing that the time had come, he told his disciples, "Since I first resided here, I have beheld the sacred countenance three times;
now I behold it once more. It is certain that I shall be born in the Pure Land. When the appointed time arrived, he sat upright and entered nirvana.
This was the sixth day of the eighth month. He authored the *Lushan ji* (Collection from Mount Lu) in ten fascicles.

He was the uterine younger brother of the Jin dynasty monk Hui持 (Huidi), who was a fellow disciple of Master Huiyuan. At the age of eighteen, he took Master Dao'an as his teacher and studied the various scriptures extensively.

He roamed freely through the Tripitaka and was particularly proficient in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Fan Ning, the Governor of Yuzhang, once invited the Master to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Abhidharma-śāstra*.
Students gathered from all directions like clouds. In the third year of the Long’an era, he took leave of his elder brother to enter Shu;

Huiyuan tried to detain him, but the Master said, "Since I have severed desire to seek the Way, I shall simply take the Western Land as my destination. Upon arriving in Chengdu, he resided at Longyuan Temple.
He greatly propagated the Buddha-dharma. Those who ascended his hall were said to have "climbed the Dragon Gate.

In the fourth month of the third year of the Zhihe era of the Song dynasty, Jiazhou reported that a great tree had been broken by the wind and that a monk was in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). By imperial decree, he was sent to the capital.

In the eighth month, he entered the Inner Translation Institute (*Yijingyuan*), where he struck a metal gong to emerge from his absorption. The monk said, "I am Huidi, the younger brother of Master Yuan of Donglin."
He traveled west to Mount Emei and entered meditative absorption there. When asked where he intended to go, he replied, "Chenliu. He then entered absorption once more.

Emperor Huizong ordered his portrait to be painted and distributed, and composed a eulogy for it, which says: "The ancient patriarch of seven hundred years past— Who could know the news from within his samādhi?
How can this compare to departing westward with a single shoe? Birth and death are but vain toil; wood serves as skin."
The Jin dynasty monk Sengrui was a native of Jizhou. He traveled to study in various regions and journeyed throughout the territories of India.

Upon returning to Guanzhong, he sought instruction on the meaning of the sutras from Kumārajīva. When Kumārajīva was translating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he encountered the passage by Dharmarakṣa’s version which reads:
"Heaven sees man; man sees heaven. Kumārajīva remarked, "This phrasing is overly literal. Sengrui said, "Could it not mean that humans and devas meet one another?"
The two were able to meet, and Kumārajīva was delighted; he subsequently adopted [Dao’an’s] text. Later, he entered Mount Lu to rely upon Master Huiyuan and cultivate the practice of purity.
Thereafter, he traveled to the capital and resided at Wuyi Temple, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*; those who heard him were moved by his teachings and submitted to his authority.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he passed away while facing west with palms joined. The assembly saw a golden lotus flower before his couch, which suddenly vanished.
Five-colored fragrant smoke issued forth from within the room.
Shi Fachong of Shan East during the Jin dynasty was surnamed Zhu. He entered the Way in his youth and was renowned for his observance of the precepts.

He was devoted to the sutras and śāstras, and was particularly proficient in the *Lotus Sūtra*. Once, while traveling at Lushan in Xiangzhou, a mountain spirit transformed into a celestial being and approached the Master to request [instruction].

Regarding his precepts: he donated the mountain where he resided to establish a monastery. After the Master had lived there for a short time, his transformation of others permeated the region of Xiang.

Later, he returned to Mount Gexian, where he dwelt in a thatched hut, drinking from mountain streams, finding joy in dhyāna and wisdom. He authored the *Fahua yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) in four fascicles.

Shi Daorong of Pengcheng Commandery in the Jin dynasty followed Master Kumārajīva into the Xiaoyao Garden to participate in the detailed examination of the newly translated *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

As he established a lecture hall for its exposition, Kumārajīva himself attended, and marveled at his extraordinary talent. Together with Shi Tanying, Daorong produced commentaries on the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, both of which circulated in the world.
Master Tanying was skilled at lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as well as the *Prasphuta-pāramitā-stotra* (the *Guangzan*). Every time...
He propagated [the teachings], and his audience numbered in the thousands; he also assisted Kumārajīva in translating the scriptures and was held in high esteem.

The Jin monk Tanyi was a native of Yuhang. Initially, while the śramaṇa Fazhi was constantly reciting the Lotus Sūtra, a pheasant would fly and perch at the corner of his seat as if listening to the sutra.
After seven years, the pheasant died, and Fazhi buried it. That night, he dreamed of a young boy who bowed to him and said:
Because he had heard the sutras, he was liberated from his life as a bird and was now born into the Wang family before the mountains.
One day, when the Wang family prepared a vegetarian feast, Hui-zhi went to their door. The child said, "I have come with Master Hui-shang.

Zhi stroked him and said, "This is my pheasant-child. He removed his robe and looked under his arm; indeed, there were three feathers of a pheasant. Consequently, he named him Yi (Wing). At the age of seven, he left the household life.
At sixteen, he shaved his head and first entered Mount Lu to rely upon Master Huiyuan. Subsequently, he went to Guanzhong to study under Kumārajīva.
In the thirteenth year of the Yixi era, he returned east to Kuaiji, where he entered Qinwang Mountain and built a thatched hut called the Fahua Jing-she (Lotus Blossom Hermitage).
There he specialized in the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra. Twelve years later, a woman dressed in colorful garments appeared, carrying a basket containing a large white pig.

She brought two stalks of garlic and went before the Master, saying, "I entered the mountains to gather ferns, and now day turns to evening. Wolves and jackals roam everywhere; there is no way for me to return home.
I venture to beg for one night's lodging. The Master declined her most earnestly, but the woman wailed on and on. He finally allowed her to stay upon a straw bed.
At midnight, she cried out in pain, saying her belly hurt, and asked the Master to massage her. The Master wrapped his tin staff in cloth and [reached out] from afar...
He pressed down upon them. The following day, the woman transformed into auspicious clouds in her colorful robes; the pig changed into a white elephant; and the garlic blossomed into twin lotuses.
They ascended into the air, and she said to the Master, "I am the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Since you will soon return to my assembly, I came specifically to test you and observe your mind. It is like the moon in water—incapable of being defiled. Thereafter...

The heavens rained down flowers, and the earth shook everywhere. Just as Governor Meng Ji was rising from his bed to attend to affairs at dawn, he suddenly beheld auspicious clouds in the south, their radiance streaming across the courtyard.
Recognizing this as the manifestation of Samantabhadra, he reported it to the court.
An imperial edict was issued to establish Fahua Temple—which is today’s Tianyi Temple. After the Master had passed away, his body was lacquered and preserved within the mountains.
Shi Fakuang, whose secular surname was Gao, resided at Waguan Monastery in the capital of Jin. His character and conduct were exceptionally eminent.
Once, while performing ritual repentance for his master, on the seventh day he was moved by a five-colored radiance that illuminated the chamber; the ailment he suffered immediately abated.

Later, he resided in a stone grotto on Mount Qing at Qian. He often remarked that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains the principle of unifying the three vehicles, while the *Amitāyus-sūtra* is the cause for the Pure Land;
he frequently chanted these two scriptures. When Xie An served as the Governor of Wuxing, he constantly went to pay his respects to him.

Emperor Jianwen summoned him to inquire after his well-being. At that time, a comet had appeared, and the Emperor consulted the Master regarding it. The Master performed sincere repentance and rituals of expiation; shortly thereafter, the star vanished.
During the Xingning era, he traveled east to Ruyi, staying at Changyuan Temple. He rescued those suffering from illness and hardship, responding to their needs as surely as an echo.
People often saw dozens of spirits flanking and guarding the Master while he was walking or sitting.
Shi Faxu of Shishushan in Western Shu during the Jin dynasty was a native of Gaochang. His virtuous conduct was pure and prudent; he maintained a vegetarian diet and practiced dhyāna.

Later, he entered Shu and dwelt among the tombs of Liu Shi. He practiced dhūta austerities in the mountain valleys; even when tigers and rhinoceroses saw him, they did not harm him. He recited the three sutras:

the Lotus Sutra, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra, and the Prabhāsa Sūtra. He once resided in a stone grotto, where he alternated between meditation and recitation. Suddenly, in the height of summer, his right...

He passed away while leaning against a pillar; for seven days his body did not decay. The local people erected a stūpa for him, which emitted light one night that illuminated several *li* in every direction.
The Jin monk Fayi, surnamed Zhu, entered the path at the age of seven and devoted himself to the study of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Later, he left the capital and extensively established lecture halls.
During the Xingning era, he returned to Jiangzuo and stayed at the Baoshan Vihāra in Kuaiji. In the second year of the Xian’an era, he suddenly...

He fell ill, yet he continued reciting the sutras without ceasing and constantly maintained mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara. One night, he dreamed of a practitioner who extracted his intestines and stomach to wash away their impurities.
Once cleansed, the practitioner returned them to his abdomen. Upon waking, he was immediately healed.
In the second year of the Jianxing era of the Jin dynasty, more than one hundred li west of Changsha County, two stalks of blue lotuses grew upon dry land.

Monastics and laypeople vied with one another to view them; they subsequently excavated the ground for a depth of one zhang and two chi, discovering an earthenware shrine from which the lotuses had emerged through the ruins.
They broke it open to examine it; there were the roots and stalks of a blue lotus growing amidst the skull and teeth-bones.
An elder said, "In the past, there was a monk of unknown name who recited the Lotus Sutra more than ten thousand times. He passed away without illness. This must be his remains.
Consequently, the community established a temple there named Waguan (Potter’s Office).

Liu Chengzhi, style name Zhongsu, was a native of Pengcheng during the Jin dynasty. Having initially donned his official robes as a military aide (*canjun*) in the provincial administration, he entered Mount Lu and devoted himself wholeheartedly to the community there.

The court conferred upon him the title "The Relic Man" (*Yimin*). Together with Master Huiyuan, Lei Cizong, Zhou Xuzhi, Zong Bing, Zhang Quan, and others, he formed the Lotus Society to collectively cultivate the Pure Land.
They engraved their vows upon stone and composed the *Nianfo sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection).

The *Samādhi-poem* reveals the intent of his single-minded seated meditation. Within half a year, while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he saw the Buddha’s light illuminating the ground, all of which turned the color of gold.
After fifteen years, while recollecting the Buddha, he beheld Amitābha Buddha;

the light from his jade-like brow shone forth as he comforted him and touched the crown of his head. One day, while recollecting the Buddha, he again saw himself entering a pool of the seven treasures, where lotuses...
The flowers were blue and white, and the water was deep and clear. A man with a halo around his neck and a *svastika* on his chest pointed to the pond water and said, "This is water of eight virtues;
you may drink from it. Cheng drank the water, and its sweetness and excellence were extraordinary.

Upon waking, he still perceived a rare fragrance emanating from his pores. He sighed and said, "The conditions for my rebirth in the Pure Land have now arrived. He then invited monks to perform a turning of the Dharma wheel.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* several hundred times. Subsequently, when the monks from Mount Lu had all assembled, Chengzhi burned incense before the images, prostrated himself twice, and made this vow:
"By means of the Bequeathed Teaching of Śākyamuni, I have come to know that there is Amitābha, my compassionate father.
This incense shall first be offered to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; next, it shall be offered to Amitābha Buddha; and thereafter, it shall be offered to the *Saddharma*."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Because he was able to be reborn in the Pure Land by virtue of upholding this sūtra, may all sentient beings likewise be reborn there.
Facing west with palms joined, he passed away; it was the sixth year of the Yixi era. A wondrous fragrance wafted intensely for seven days before subsiding.
Master Huiyuan composed an inscription to commemorate his virtues.
Guṇavarman (translated into Chinese as Guǒngdé Kǎi) was a śramaṇa from the kingdom of Kaśmīra during the Song dynasty. He left the household life and received the precepts at the age of twenty.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and various other sūtras, totaling over one million words. In the first year of the Yuánjiā era, he arrived in Guangzhou on a merchant vessel with a favorable wind.

Emperor Wén heard of him and issued an edict for the provincial and commandery authorities to provide him with provisions and escort. His route passed through Shìxīng, where he halted at Hǔmén Temple.
At Fushan, he established a separate meditation hall outside the mountain temple. Although the mountain was frequently plagued by tigers, from then on, travelers passed without obstruction;
even when they encountered a tiger, he would simply press its head down with his staff and it would depart.

Once, while sitting in meditation in the separate hall, a novice went to visit him and saw a white lion standing against a pillar. It pervaded the entire room, and blue lotus flowers grew [from its body], their radiance brilliant.

His eyes were stolen away. The śrāmaṇera cried out in alarm, and suddenly he could see nothing at all. In the first month of the eighth year, he arrived in Jiankang and was ordered by imperial decree to reside at Qihuan Temple, where he began lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
His subtle discernment was celestial and transcendent; all who heard him attained understanding and awakening. That summer, he resided at Dinglin Temple.

At that time, there was a believer who gathered flowers to spread over the seats; however, only upon the seat where the Master sat did the flowers become even more brilliantly colored. The assembly [marveled].

All acclaimed him as one who had realized the holy state. Shi Daosheng of the Song dynasty was a native of Julu. In his youth, he left the household life under Zhu Fatai. He first entered Mount Lu and lived in seclusion there for seven years.
At that time, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. He once held that the essential means for entering the Way is rooted in wisdom and understanding; thus, he applied himself to...

He looked up to the various scriptures and did not shrink from weariness or hardship. He traveled to Guanzhong to receive the teachings of Kumārajīva; his inquiries were exceptionally brilliant, and all praised him for his divine insight.
Later, while lecturing on the sutras at Mount Huqiu, when he reached the passage stating that even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, the stubborn rocks all nodded their heads.
Furthermore, while reciting the Lotus Sutra at Bantang, a young boy followed him to leave the household life and likewise began to recite it.
In the Dharma Flower [Era], a youth passed away and was buried in a forest. One night, the sound of him reciting a sutra was heard.

The local people found this extraordinary and opened his grave to investigate; they discovered a tongue from which a blue lotus flower had grown. Consequently, a stupa was erected there, and later it was developed into a temple.
(Now known as Bantang Temple) Gao Qi composed a poem in praise [of this site], which says: Yellow earth may bury the bones, but how could it bury the spirit?
I have heard that once amidst the overgrown weeds, a blue lotus once bloomed. The body has returned to the long night’s abode, yet the mouth recites the Western Scripture.

Seeking its traces, they are profoundly remote; hearing its voice, it is ever clear and resonant. A cold lamp illuminates the empty stupa, where from time to time a mountain monk comes to listen. It should be responded to.
He caused those in neighboring graves to hear [the Dharma], and all who were immersed in delusion were awakened.
Shi Fazhuang of the Song dynasty was a native of Huainan. In his youth, he became a disciple of Master Huiyuan. He was renowned for his rigorous asceticism.
Later, he traveled to Guanzhong and studied under Master Daorong. At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he resided at Daochang Temple. By nature, he was simple and unadorned, eating only at noon.
While he was reciting the *Nirvāṇa* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras, heavenly deities were frequently moved to come and listen.
Every time he chanted during the late night, those in neighboring rooms would constantly hear the sound of soldiers and guards providing a protective escort before his chamber.

The Song dynasty monk Shi Huiqing, surnamed Zhu, was a native of Guangling. He resided at Mount Lu Monastery, where his mastery of the sutras and vinaya was profound; he was pure and possessed strict observance of the precepts.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Suyāma-sūtra*, and other scriptures, chanting them every night. One night, while he was reciting, he heard the sound of finger-snapping and voices of praise coming from the darkness.

During the Yuanjia era, while crossing the Yangtze River, he encountered a storm and his boat was on the verge of capsizing; the Master continued his recitation without ceasing, remaining conscious throughout.
A boat was in the midst of the waves; facing the wind and cutting through the current, it felt as if someone were pulling it, and in an instant it reached the shore.
Shi Daojiong of Nanjian Temple in the capital of the Song dynasty was a native of Fufeng.

Because his master was ill, he and three companions entered Mount Huo in Henan to collect stalactites. After exploring the cave for several li, the three men drowned and their torches went out. Daojiong—
He silently recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and, with sincere devotion, prayed for deliverance. He also kept Avalokiteśvara in his thoughts. After a short while, he saw a light like that of fireflies;
he pursued it and was thus able to escape from the cave. Later, when he performed a feast offering for Samantabhadra, two monks came to pay homage to the Buddha;
as they were leaving the gate, they flew through the air and departed. Everyone was struck with wonder and marvel.
The Song dynasty monk Shi Tandi was surnamed Kang. His ancestors were natives of Kangju, who migrated to China at the end of the Han dynasty and later settled in Wuxing.
His father, Tang, served as the Vice Director of Jizhou.

While his mother, Lady Huang, was napping during the day, she dreamed that a monk called out to her as "Mother," entrusting her with a *zhuchi* whisk, along with two iron-inlaid book-weights. Upon waking, she found both objects still there. Thereupon...
When the Master was five years old, his mother showed him a fly-whisk and other objects. The Master said, "These were gifts from the King of Qin.

His mother asked, "Where did you put them? He replied, "I have forgotten. At the age of ten, he left home to become a monk. His learning did not depend on a teacher; his realization arose spontaneously from Heaven.

Regarding the profound principles of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, his eloquence flowed like a cascading river. Once, while accompanying his father to the region between Fandeng and Deng, he encountered a monk from Guanzhong.
When he met the monk Daoshi, the Master suddenly called out Daoshi’s name. Daoshi asked, “Why do you, a young novice, call an elder by his name?

The Master replied, “In the past, when I was the śrāmaṇera Ti, I was gathering vegetables for the assembly of monks when I was wounded by a wild boar. Now that I have unexpectedly encountered you, I could not help but let my voice escape.
Daoshi had no memory of this at first, so he questioned Daotong, who recounted the beginning and end of the matter in detail and showed him [the marks].
He inscribed this upon the *zhentǔ* (dust-whisk). [Hui]qiè was enlightened by this and wept, saying: "This is the late master, Dharma Master Hongjue.
When the late master lectured on the *Lotus Sutra* for Yao Chang, I served as the assistant lecturer (*dūjiǎng*). Yao Chang presented these two items to the late master.

As I reflect upon the passing of Hongjue, it is precisely the day he entrusted these objects to me. Furthermore, remembering the incident of gathering wild vegetables, my grief and veneration increase all the more. The Master—
In his later years, he entered Wuqiu Temple in Wu, where he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* fifteen times each.

Later, he returned to Wuxing, where he lived in seclusion, subsisting on water from mountain streams for over twenty years. Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, he manifested his passing at the mountain.
The Song dynasty monk Shi Tansui resided at the Baima Monastery in Heyin. He lived in simple cloth robes and maintained a vegetarian diet, reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* once every day.

Once, in the middle of the night, he suddenly heard a voice knocking at his door, saying, "We request that you preach the Dharma for us for ninety days. The Master did not grant permission; however, when they insisted, he finally agreed.
While still in the midst of sleep, he was unaware that his body had already arrived within the shrine of the White Horse Mound deity. And so it was.
The disciple remained with him at all times. From then on, he went there daily in secret, with no one knowing of it.
Later, as the temple monks were passing before the shrine, they saw two high seats: the Master sat to the north and the disciple to the south, appearing as if engaged in a lecture.
They also smelled a wondrous fragrance. Thereupon, they spread word of this divine marvel until the summer retreat had ended.

Shi Puming of the Song dynasty was from the Zhang family of Linzi. He entered the monastic order in his youth. By nature he was pure and sincere, making the practice of repentance and recitation his vocation.
He recited the Lotus Sūtra, for which he maintained separate clothing and a separate seat, never allowing them to become defiled or mixed with the mundane.
Whenever he reached the "Chapter on Exhortation and Inspiration," he would invariably see Samantabhadra riding a six-tusked elephant appear before him.
The Song dynasty monk Shi Baotong cultivated the pure life with great diligence. He regularly recited the "Dhāraṇī Chapter" of the Lotus Sūtra, and after a long time, miraculous responses appeared.
At that time, there was a woman of the Zhao clan in Yangqiao Village who was possessed by a malevolent spirit; she requested the Master to recite the "Dhāraṇī Chapter."

A deity manifested its form and summoned the ghost to receive reprimand. Zhao’s wife recovered. Later, when the illness recurred, the Master went there and saw the ghost he had previously reprimanded standing before him.
The Master said, "I have already warned you and punished you; why have you come back?

I shall now recite a mantra to cause your head to split into seven pieces, like the branches of an *ari* tree. The ghost bowed its head and piteously begged to depart, whereupon the illness was finally cured.
The Song dynasty monk Shi Sengdeng resided at Dailin Monastery on Mount Lu. He was proficient in reciting the Lotus Sūtra, doing so day and night without ceasing.
One day, he suddenly saw a silver palace in the sky gradually descend toward his room; it then transformed into a golden palace. The Master subsequently entered the palace.

He sat, rose, and practiced walking meditation in this manner for three years. People from far and near followed his transformation; he preached the precepts to them, and light emanated from his mouth.
One day, returning from outside, he said to his disciples, "Now I shall ascend the golden hall and never emerge again. He then passed away with serene detachment.
A wondrous fragrance filled the air for an entire month.
The Song dynasty monk Shi Fahui was originally surnamed Xiahou. He maintained his resolve with refined austerity, and his observance of the Vinaya was as strict as ice.

Toward the end of the Daming era, he traveled east to explore the Cave of Yu (Yuxue) and took up residence on Mount Tianzhu, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra once every day; his aspirations were deeply absorbed in the realm beyond the mundane world.
He resided in his tower for over thirty years. Princes and nobles who arrived there would merely dismount their carriages, pay their respects at the gate, and return;
only Zhou Yong of Runan, whose faith and understanding were both profound, was specially received by him. Wherever he recited the sutras, colored clouds would constantly envelop the space above.

The Song dynasty monk Shi Hui-liang enjoyed a reputation for purity from his youth. He established a monastery in Linzi and lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Students gathered like clouds from as far as a thousand li, traveling there on horseback. Later, he crossed the Yangtze River and resided at Heyuan Monastery.

Yan Yanzhi and Zhang Xu held him in high esteem and remained in his company, often sighing in admiration: "Tanyuan and Fa’ai emitted pearls and jade before us; Tanbin and Hui-liang vibrate with golden sounds behind us. His character was pure.
Regarding his "Wondrous Enlightenment" (Miaowu), it was nearly lost but has been restored; he composed the *Xuántōng lùn* (Treatise on Mysterious Penetration), which circulates in the world.
The monk Huìguǒ of Yangzhou during the Song dynasty disciplined himself with a vegetarian diet from his youth. During the Taishi era, he traveled to the capital and resided at Waguan Monastery.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*. Once, by the side of a latrine, he saw a ghost who paid him homage and said, "In the past, I was a member of the assembly..."

A monk who served as the *karmadāna* (Vina) was slightly deficient in accordance with the Dharma and consequently fell among the ghosts of latrines. The Dharma Master, out of compassion, hoped to deliver him.

There were three thousand coins buried beneath a persimmon tree; he wished for them to be taken for the sake of merit. The Master informed the assembly to dig up the money and commissioned a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Later, the ghost appeared again in a dream and said, "Having received the power of your compassion, I have already attained rebirth. He then offered his thanks and departed.
Formerly, there was the monk Shi Huiyi of Guangling in the capital of the Song dynasty. During the Xiaojian era, he resided at Zhulin Monastery.

He recited the Lotus Sūtra and practiced asceticism with diligent devotion, vowing to burn his own body in emulation of the deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. The Emperor sent an envoy to dissuade him, but he would not listen.
In the seventh year of the Daming era, on the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth, he went to the palace gate to take leave of the Emperor and entrusted him with the Buddha-dharma.
He then established an oil cauldron at Mount Zhong, wrapped his body in cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), and personally held a candle to set it ablaze while reciting the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" chapter.

When the fire reached his eyes, his voice finally ceased. At that moment, the sound of flutes and pipes was heard, and a wondrous fragrance wafted abroad. That night, the Emperor dreamed that the Master once again entrusted him with [the Dharma].

He was entrusted with the protection of the Dharma. On the following day, a great assembly was convened. By imperial decree, Yaowang Temple was established at the site where he had performed self-immolation.
The Song dynasty monk Sengyu was a native of Yuhang. Initially, he built the Zhaoti Vihāra on the southern ridge of Mount Lu. He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra.

In the sixth month of the second year of the Xiaojian era, he said to the assembly: "The accumulation of karmic bonds within the three miserable realms is due to the nature of emotional attachment. Emotional..."

"My life is coming to an end; my physical form should likewise be relinquished. How could the path of the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) be so far away? He then took leave of the assembly and entered a thatched hut.

Sitting upright, he recited the "Chapter on the Self-Immolation of the Medicine King" from the Lotus Sutra. He lit a torch to set himself ablaze. When the multitude saw purple vapors ascending into the sky, after ten days, twin paulownia trees grew at the site of the cremation.
Those who understood signs declared this to be an omen of the twin *śāla* trees [under which the Buddha passed away].
The Song dynasty nun Huiyu was a native of Chang’an. She resided at Muniu Monastery in Jiangling and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and other scriptures;
within ten days, she had mastered them all. During the Yuanjia era, she burned incense and prostrated before the Buddha, vowing:

“If my sincere heart moves the divine response, may I behold a Buddha-land after casting off this body. Within seven days, I pray to see the light of the Buddha. On the fifth night, to the east of the monastery...
In the forest trees, a radiant sign suddenly appeared, its form and color blazing brilliantly; the multitude marveled at this rare occurrence.
During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the nun Daoshou recited the Lotus Sūtra three thousand times.
Each time she did so, she saw a luminous jeweled canopy in the sky hanging down to cover the crown of her head.

Fei Shi, wife of Luo Yu of Shudu in the Song dynasty, had recited the Lotus Sūtra since her youth with such diligence that she never grew weary. Later, she suffered from heart pain and was on the verge of death;
as the final breaths were being drawn and she awaited the end, she suddenly dreamed of a Buddha’s hand rubbing her heart. She recovered instantly.
All members of her household beheld a golden light and also smelled a fragrant aroma.
The nun Zhitong of Jianjing Temple in the Song dynasty abandoned her precepts and married Qunfu of the Liang family. After seven years, their son was born.

As the family was poor and lacked clothing, she remembered that during her time as a nun she possessed a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* written on plain silk. She immediately boiled and pounded it to make a garment for her son to wear.

Suddenly, sores broke out all over his body; white worms crawled over and bit him incessantly. He wailed for ten days before he died. A voice was heard from the air saying: "Because you violated the precepts, you have now fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts."

It is said that by tearing up scriptures to make clothing, one receives this as a "flower-retribution" (hua-bao), while the actual fruit is to be experienced in hell. This was also an event from the Yuanjia period.
Wang Xuanmo of Taiyuan Qi served under the Song dynasty; during the Yuanjia era, he lost his command while leading a northern expedition, and Xiao Bin intended to execute him.
Shen Qingzhi remonstrated, saying, "Fuli (the childhood name of Emperor Shizu of the Wei dynasty) has his majesty shaking the world; how could Xuánmó possibly withstand him?
Furthermore, by killing your generals, you are merely weakening yourself. Thereupon, [Xuánmó] desisted. Initially, when Xuánmó was about to be executed, he dreamed that a person told him:
"If one can recite the Avalokiteśvara Divine Mantra from the 'Universal Gate' chapter of the Lotus Sutra one thousand times, one may be spared. Once he had awakened, he recited it without ceasing;
suddenly, a report arrived that the execution had been stayed. Later, his official rank reached that of a Grand Marshal (Kaifu).
In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, there was a resident of the capital named Sun Yanzeng, whose family had for generations been devoted to Buddhism.

He had a concubine, Wang Huicheng, who regularly recited the Lotus Sūtra. One day, she suddenly saw a light at the river’s edge; upon digging there, she discovered a golden Buddha statue. It originally bore an inscription stating:
"The sixth year of Jianwu, the Gengzi year, fashioned by the monk Faxin of the government monastery. It appears that this Faxin was the concubine’s...

In the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, there was the monk Shi Huijin of Gaosuo Temple in Yangzhou. A native of Wuxing, he had been bold and martial, devoted to the ways of the *xianxia* (wandering knights) in his youth.

At the age of forty, he suddenly awakened to the extraordinary nature of reality and consequently left the household life. Wearing simple robes and subsisting on vegetarian fare, he vowed to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, applying himself with single-minded devotion.

He applied himself with diligent effort, yet whenever he took up his scrolls, he would fall ill. He then made a vow to produce one hundred copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in order to repent for his prior karmic obstructions.
Once his vow was fulfilled, his illness was completely cured. Later, he vowed to dedicate the merit of his recitation toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
He heard a voice from the air saying, "Your vow is already fulfilled; you shall certainly attain rebirth. At over eighty years of age, he passed away peacefully without any illness.
Shi Hongming of Qi was a native of Kuaiji. He was upright, austere, and possessed a resolute character.

During the Yongming era, he resided at Yunmen Temple in Shan-yin, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra and practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without slackening during the six periods of the day. Every morning, the water in his pitcher would fill itself;
it was truly celestial youths who served as his attendants. Whenever he sat in meditation, tigers would often crouch inside his room, beholding the Master sitting with dignified composure.
He remained motionless. After a long time, he finally departed.
Shi Fakui of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Wan; he was a native of Yuqian in Wuxing. He entered the monastic order at Zhiyuan Temple and maintained himself with simple integrity.

He did not involve himself in worldly affairs and constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Whenever he received offerings during vegetarian assemblies, he would set aside the funds to create a sandalwood Buddha image.
Once the image was completed, he personally organized a great assembly for its consecration. His family resided in the capital;

on the morning of that day, they returned home, while he went to Dinglin Monastery and subsequently returned to Zhiguan Monastery. Later, when the three locations were investigated, it was found that the Master had been at all three places for his midday meal at one and the same time.
He visited three locations on that same day. That evening, he returned to his quarters and passed away suddenly; his body was remarkably fragrant and supple, and two fingers remained bent.
The assembly all realized that he had attained the fruit of sainthood, and consequently built a pagoda at Zhiyuan Temple. This was during the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty.
Shi Huiyu of the Qi dynasty was a native of Huanglong. He traveled to the capital and resided at Linggen Monastery, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra as a bridge for rescuing those in suffering.
Once, in his quarters, he saw three men knocking at the door; they were all dressed in fresh and clean robes and caps, and each held a flowered parasol.
Huiyu asked what they were doing, and they replied, "The Dharma Master is due to enter nirvana, so we have come to welcome you. Huiyu said, "This is but a small matter."
The plan was not realized. [The master] asked, "May I extend it for one more year? He replied, "It may be so. When the term expired the following year, he passed away without illness.
This was the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty; he was fifty-seven years of age.

Shi Chaobian of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Zhang. A native of Dunhuang, he possessed profound spiritual insight from childhood and was naturally serene. He made the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* his daily practice.
Hearing that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing greatly in the capital, he traveled from Ba and Chu to Jianye, where he resided at Dinglin Temple.

There he lived in seclusion, sitting against a wall for over thirty years. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* with a daily limit of one complete reading; his mind was so agile that his speech followed effortlessly. He was constant...

He possessed further spiritual power. In the tenth year of the Yongming era, he manifested his passing into nirvana. Vinaya Master Sengyou erected a stele for him, with Liu Xie of Dongguan composing the inscription.
Not long after, a single branch of a blue lotus flower grew from his burial site.
Shi Huiji of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Lü. A native of Qiantang in Wu, he entered the monastic order at age fifteen at Zhihuan Temple.

He was rigorous in his practice and ascetic in his discipline, excelling in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Small Version) and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Later, he resided at Fahua Temple in Shanyin, where he lectured on and propagated the scriptures and teachings;

students flocked to him like deer. He subsequently established the Baolin Vihāra in Huaiyi, where he dreamed that Samantabhadra emitted light to welcome and guide him; consequently, he constructed [an image of] Samantabhadra.

The image of the Sage, together with the form of a six-tusked white elephant, was [erected]. Prince Jingling once inquired of him regarding the essential points of the *Lotus Sūtra*, whereupon he composed the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* in three fascicles.
In the third year of the Jianwu era, he manifested illness.
His disciples dreamed of several Brahmā monks sitting cross-legged upon the steps, saying, "We have come from the Mahāyāna country to welcome Master Ji. Thereupon, he passed away peacefully.
Shi Senghou of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Gong. A native of Xiliangzhou, he entered the monastic order in his youth and immediately demonstrated a rigorous commitment to ascetic discipline.
He traveled to the capital, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* once every two days for over sixty years, never ceasing his practice of meditation and recitation.

He built a dwelling on the rear ridge as a place for meditative seclusion; it was constantly filled with extraordinary fragrances and exotic flowers of unknown origin. When people climbed [the hill]...
Her door was solemn and reverent, as if a hidden force had been stirred; it was said that the deities of her precepts were secretly protecting her.

In the second year of the Yongyuan era, she suffered from a slight illness and ceased eating. She then sought water to rinse her mouth, joined her palms, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away at the age of eighty-nine.

Xiao Ziliang, Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty, styled Yunying, was sincere in his sense of righteousness and fond of antiquity. He had read extensively through the classics and scriptures; the world hailed him as a "sea of calligraphy.
Together with Crown Prince Wenhui, he was both refined in the principles of Buddhism. He frequently summoned renowned monks to lecture on various sūtras and vehicles (*yāna*).
The grandeur of his reverence for the Dharma was unprecedented on the left bank of the Yangtze River. At times, he personally served food and distributed water to the assembly of monks, and recited—

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* moved him deeply, and his refined and sublime compositions were akin to those of Chen Si (Wang Xizhi). He authored the twenty-fascicle *Jingzhuzi* (Disciples of Pure Abiding), which has circulated in the world.
"Pure abiding" (*jingzhu*) is the Chinese translation of the Sanskrit term *poṣadha*, meaning to abide in accordance with the precepts by purifying one's body, speech, and mind.

Liu Qiu (style name Lingyu) of the Qi dynasty was a native of Nanyang. He possessed profound faith in the teachings of Śākyamuni; he wore coarse cloth and paid homage to the Buddha, observing the perpetual fast and reciting scriptures without fail during the six periods of the day.
At the beginning of the Jianyuan era, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as a Tongzhi Sanqishi Lang, but he did not accept the appointment.

He annotated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and personally lectured on the meaning of the Buddha’s teachings. In the second year of the Jianwu era, he was summoned to serve as a Guozibo.
He moved his residence to the western sandbars of Jiangling. One winter day at midday, a white cloud suddenly appeared, hovering within the eaves and doors of his quarters.
There was also a wondrous fragrance and the sound of bells and chanting. He sat upright and passed away.
The Liang dynasty monk Shi Huiyue was surnamed Lou. A native of Wushang in Dongyang, he gathered sand to build stupas and stacked stones to form seats while still a child.

At the age of seventeen, he received the tonsure. Zhou Yong, the Magistrate of Shan, treated him with exceptional courtesy and respect. He established Caotang Temple on Mount Zhong and invited the Master to reside there.
Chu Yuan, the Grand Chancellor, and Wang Jian, the Grand Marshal, requested the Master to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
He extensively propagated the teachings of the Mahāyāna sūtras. Once, while he was resting during the day after falling ill, he saw a Brahman monk who said, "A Bodhisattva is about to arrive;
the practitioner who comes next shall be him. Shortly thereafter, the Master arrived, and his illness was suddenly and completely cured. By nature, he was devoted to meditation and recitation.
A rare fragrance was sensed entering the chamber, and fierce beasts became docile at the steps. He once entered the Crimson Pine Gorge on Mount Jinhua, where he instructed the divine spirits;
consequently, the chi-mei demons ceased their disturbances. During the Tianjian era, the Emperor received the Bodhisattva precepts from him, as did the imperial princesses, both monastics and laity.
A total of forty-eight thousand people received the registers. Once, during the time he was receiving the precepts, a male magpie ascended the steps;
only after the ceremony concluded did it fly away. Furthermore, two peacocks walked slowly to the altar, bowed their necks, and listened to the Dharma.
In the first year of the Datong era, he passed away while seated in meditation. A stupa was erected to mark his tomb on its left side.

Shi Fayun of the Liang dynasty was of the Zhou family from Yangxian; he entered the monastic order at the age of seven. He was exceptionally brilliant and outstanding, and he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

He refined his studies and accumulated reflections for many years. At the age of thirty, while lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* at Miaoyin Temple, his eloquence and discernment were as vibrant as a rising breeze, and students flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel.
He also once lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* at Guangzhai Temple, when he was suddenly moved by celestial flowers filling the sky and falling like drifting snow.
At that time, Master Zhi’s realization transcended the mundane world; whenever he came to Yun’s location, he would invariably stay for two nights.
He was known as Dharma Master Dali. Once he said, "I wish to explain the Lion’s Roar. The Master (Sengzhao) immediately ascended the seat and analyzed it for him.
Sengzhi snapped his fingers in praise, saying, "Excellent! How subtle and wondrous! At the home of Yuan Ang, the Court Gentleman, there was once a monk who had been provided with offerings.

He made a vow, desiring his understanding to equal that of Master Shi Hui. One night, he suddenly dreamed of a monk who said, "Master Yun, during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, already lectured on this sutra;
how could you possibly catch up to him?"
Dharma Master Yun Guang of the Liang dynasty’s lineage is unknown. In the second year of the Putong era, he was summoned by imperial decree to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra* within the inner palace;
celestial flowers rained down. During the Tianjian era, when the Emperor suffered from a severe drought, he questioned Master Zhi about it.

The Master replied, "Yun can bring forth rain. Consequently, the Emperor invited him to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*. When the passage reached the point where the moisture universally permeates all things, it rained heavily; high and low lands were all sufficiently moistened.
Shi Daolin of the Liang dynasty was a native of Shanyin. He possessed strict observance of the precepts and was skilled in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Zhang Xu of the Wu kingdom paid him homage and served him. During the Tianjian era, he resided at Quanlin Temple in Fuyang. The temple was haunted by malevolent spirits, but upon the Master’s arrival, the ghosts immediately vanished.
His disciple Huishao was crushed by a collapsing building, and his head was forced into his chest; the Master recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for him in prayer.
At night, Yao dreamed of two foreign monks who pulled his head out from him. By morning, he had recovered. Everyone marveled at this divine response.
The Liang dynasty monk Shi Faling, surnamed Yan, was a native of Zhijiang. He left the household life at Yquan Mountain Temple and constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. He divided [the text]...
He ate but one meal a day and remained constantly seated without lying down. Carrying his mendicant’s staff, he traveled far and wide to Mount Lu, Mount Tai, Mount Heng, and Mount Luofu;

there was no distance too great for him to reach. He dwelt in remote crags, single-mindedly devoted to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Once, while traveling to Mount Dai, he passed through Xuzhou.

The county magistrate asked for official credentials, but the Master stopped and produced only a single volume of the *Lotus Sūtra*. The magistrate grew angry and imprisoned him; seven days passed without...

While eating, his voice did not carry when reciting the sutras, which caused him to experience bad dreams. He then prostrated himself in repentance. Later, he returned to seclusion and made the practice of meditation and recitation his vocation.
At the time of his death, extraordinary fragrances filled the air, only subsiding after ten days.

Shi Farin of the Liang dynasty was a native of Jiangling. He initially entered the monastic order at Tianhuang Temple. He recited and upheld the *Lotus Sūtra*, completing two full recitations every day.
Because the assembly there was large and noisy, he traveled west to the foot of Fuzhou Cliff to practice *dhūta* in solitude.

For over thirty years, he lived on wood and wore hemp garments, possessing nothing more than tattered rags. Having found his own seclusion in the deep forest, he sought no external protection, subsisting on a single meal a day. Seven...
One day, he sat in the lotus posture and contemplated his mind. Later, he passed away in the northern cave, reclining on his right side.
Shi Sengqian of Jingzhou during the Liang dynasty was a native of Wu. From childhood, he was spiritually gifted and was marveled at by Wang Xi, the Palace Attendant.
He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra, reaching more than six thousand fascicles. One day, while dozing, he dreamed of the Great Being Samantabhadra, whose body was radiant with fragrance.
Zhaozhu personally rubbed his head in blessing. He kept this secret and did not transmit it; only when he was about to pass away did he reveal it to his fellow practitioners.
He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and other sutras dozens of times each, composing commentaries for all of them that have been passed down.
During the Liang dynasty, there was a nun from Wuxing named Daoji, styled Zongchi. She received the Dharma from Bodhidharma and lived in seclusion on Mount Bian in Huzhou.
Day and night she recited the *Lotus Sūtra* until she had completed ten thousand volumes. She remained within the mountain for twenty years without venturing forth.

Later, she entered parinirvāṇa, and her entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the site where she had built her hut. In the first year of the Datong era, something suddenly appeared inside the stupa.
A single blue lotus flower appeared; both monastics and laypeople marveled at it. Upon opening [the mouth] to inspect it, they saw the flower had grown from the root of the tongue.
The local prefectures recorded and reported this to the throne, and by imperial decree, Fahua Temple was established.
In the city of Chuanshan in Liang, there was a nun named Faxuan who initially recited the Lotus Sūtra. While sitting or lying down, she would see canopies and parasols covering her from above.

Her parents sent her to Qiming Temple to enter the monastic life; on that very day, the canopies and parasols vanished. Thereafter, she extensively studied the sūtras and śāstras, delving deeply into their profound principles.
When Wang Yuanjian, the Prince of Heng, served as the governor of the commandery, he invited her to serve as the preceptor for the nuns at Yuecheng.

Yu Xian, courtesy name Yanbao, was a *zhengshi* (invited scholar) of the Liang dynasty. A native of Xinye, he mastered the classics and histories from his youth. By nature, he was simple and unassuming, with a particular fondness for forests and springs;
of his ten-mu residence, mountains and ponds occupied half the space. In his youth, he was on good terms with Emperor Wu.

When the Emperor raised his army, Yu was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the Secretary of the Pingxi Commandery, and later, during the Putong era, he was appointed as Palace Attendant (*huangmen shilang*), but he declined both positions. In his later years, he lived at his residence...
He established a dharma hall within his residence. Dwelling in the mountains, he subsisted on vegetarian food and performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* once every day. One night, after midnight, he saw a practitioner who called himself Master Yuan; his appearance and demeanor were extraordinary.

This man addressed Tanxian as "Master Shangxing," bestowed upon him incense, and departed. In the fourth year of the Zhongdatong era, while napping during the day, he suddenly woke with a start and said, "Master Yuan..."

He returned once more, but could not remain for long; having finished speaking, he passed away. The entire household heard a voice in the air proclaiming, "Master Shangxing has already been reborn in the Pure Land of Amitābha.
Emperor Wu revered him and issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title Master of Upright Integrity (Zhenjie).

Zhen Xuancheng of Zhongshan during the Liang dynasty was a man of broad learning and mastery in the classics and histories. He was known to Emperor Jianwen and served as a Recorder-Attendant General (*lushi canjun*).
Accompanying Xiao Chao to garrison Xiangyang, he took advantage of the abundance of troops and weapons in Jiangling to secretly send letters expressing his sincerity. Someone reported this to Chao;
however, Chao deeply believed in the Buddha-dharma and had vowed not to kill anyone who recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. Xuancheng had long been a reciter of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Flower. Because of this, she was spared from harm. Later, when Huichao saw her, he would often say, "Master Zhen truly possesses the power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the second year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, there was a nun named Senghua at Gaoyou. Her will and integrity were as pure as ice and frost;

she recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* without ceasing day or night. Later, whenever she recited one fascicle, a flower would immediately grow upon each of the nails of her right hand, appearing like—
Her fingers were covered with fine silk-like patterns; she could recite six or seven fascicles of scripture from memory. Two lotus flowers grew simultaneously upon her palms.
Emperor Wu summoned her for an audience and held her in great esteem and respect. At that time, she was consequently called "The Nun with Lotus Hands."

The Venerable Master Huisi of Nanyue, Chen, was the son of Li Wujin. From childhood, he observed the precepts and prostrated himself before the *Lotus Sūtra*, to the point of forgetting both sleep and rest.
Because of prolonged rain and dampness, his body became afflicted with edema; yet, directing his mind toward the scripture with fortitude, he was soon restored to health.
In a dream, Samantabhadra mounted a white elephant king and personally rubbed his head. A fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) emerged upon his crown.

At the age of fifteen, he left home to become a monk and received full ordination. He ate only one meal per day and specialized in reciting the Lotus Sūtra, completing more than a thousand recitations.

He was moved by the response that the water in his pitcher never ran dry, and a celestial youth attended upon him. At that time, Master Huiwen, while reading the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, reached the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths, where a verse says:
"Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I say they are emptiness; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

Upon achieving sudden and clear enlightenment, he then prostrated from afar to Nāgārjuna as his teacher. Relying on the treatise to establish his contemplation, the Master then went to transmit the Dharma to him.
Day and night he restrained his mind, never allowing his side to touch the mat. After thirty days of sitting through the summer retreat, he attained the supernormal power of recollecting past lives.
He redoubled his vigor and diligence, yet suddenly obstacles to meditation arose; his four limbs became limp and weak, and his body would not obey his mind.

He then thought to himself: "Illness arises from karma, and karma originates from the mind. If the source of the mind does not arise, what form can external objects take? Illness, karma, and the mind are all like clouds."
Having observed the shadow in this manner, his inverted perceptions were extinguished, yet his physical pliancy remained as before.
Throughout the entire year, he still attained nothing, and harboring deep inner shame, he leaned his body against a wall. Suddenly, he attained great awakening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

Thereafter, regarding sūtras he had not previously heard, he understood them spontaneously without doubt. Subsequently, at Mount Dasu in Guangzhou, he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and once received offerings.

He practiced giving. At Qiguang Temple, he commissioned the transcription of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in golden characters and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in golden characters—these two sections.
He further composed a personal vow, praying that at the time of Maitreya Buddha, his own person and these scriptures would appear simultaneously to extensively transform all beings.
In the second year of the Guangda era, he went to reside on Mount Nanyue. One day, while ascending Mount Zhurong Peak, the mountain deity requested the precepts from him.
The Master then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them. Pointing to the base of a cliff, he said, "In my first life, I sat in meditation here and was beheaded by bandits.

He then pointed to a set of dry bones (now known as the Yishengyan, or "First Life Cliff") and said, "I found these and erected a stupa to repay the kindness of my past cultivation" (now known as the Ershengta, or "Second Life Stupa").
Moving to the southwest corner, he pointed to a large rock and said, "In my second life, I also resided here. He immediately gathered the skull fragments and built a stupa.
They then arrived at a dense, secluded place, where [the Master] said, "This was an ancient temple where I resided for three lifetimes.

Have it excavated. When they dug, there were indeed monastic utensils and the foundations still remained; he immediately built a platform there and preached the Dharma to the assembly (this is the present-day Sengshengzang).

The assembly suffered from a lack of water, so the Master struck the cliff with his staff. A tiger then clawed at the earth, and a spring gushed forth. From this point on, he transformed and guided beings through the Way.
His fame grew ever more widespread. The Chen ruler treated him with exceptional courtesy, and he was then known as the Great Meditation Master Sengzhi.

In the sixth month of the ninth year of the Dajian era, he chanted the name of the Buddha, joined his palms, and passed away; a wondrous fragrance filled the room. He once addressed the assembly, saying:

"The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not remote. Seek it only within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere. If you seek it, you will not find it; even if you were to find it, it would not be the true."
Shi Xuanguang of Chen was a native of Silla. Devoted exclusively to the cultivation of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), he crossed the vast ocean to seek the methods of Chan in the Central Kingdom.
He subsequently traveled to Mount Heng to consult with Chan Master Sida, who transmitted to him the "Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss. He soon realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Upon returning to Jiangnan, he boarded a sea vessel; as they reached the great ocean, he suddenly beheld multicolored clouds, elegant music, and a flurry of ceremonial banners and insignia.
They arrived in great numbers. From the air came a call, saying, "The Heavenly Emperor summons Master Xuanguang to preach the Dharma-gate of Direct Realization within the Dragon Palace.
