The Master folded his hands and declined, but seeing a youth in green robes leading the way, he followed him into the palace city.

It was unlike any human palace or government office; on all sides were nothing but scaly creatures and beings half-human, half-divine. Once they had ascended the high terrace, he expounded the wondrous Dharma.
After seven days, the King personally escorted him off; when the Master boarded his boat again, the boatmen said it had been only half a day.
The Patriarch of Nanyue constructed a portrait hall (yingtang), within which he depicted the Master’s image; the same was done for the Patriarch Hall at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.
Chen Xu Xiaokē was a native of Shàn in Dōnghǎi. In his youth, he discussed the profound principles of metaphysics (*xuánlǐ*); as he grew older, he became proficient in the Five Classics.

At the beginning of the Tàiqīng era of the Liáng dynasty, he began his official career as a *bōshì* (lecturer) at the Imperial Academy. He was of the utmost filial piety; during the mourning for his father, he was nearly unable to endure the loss.

He served his biological mother with complete devotion to the Way. During the Tiānjiā era, he was appointed Magistrate of Shàn, but soon thereafter he resigned from office. During the Tàijiàn era, he was summoned to serve as Director of the Secretariat (*míshūchéng*).

He did not accept [the office]. He maintained a vegetarian diet and observed lifelong fasting, upholding the Bodhisattva precepts. For six years, he lectured on and recited the Lotus Sūtra day and night.

He was subsequently relieved from his post as Director of the National Academy. At the time of his death, he sat upright while reciting the Buddha’s name; an extraordinary fragrance filled the room, leaving all the neighbors struck with wonder.
The Northern Wei monk Shi Sengzhao resided at Danling Temple on Mount Tai. Whenever he traveled through mountains and rivers, he delighted in seeking out secluded and precipitous places.
In the first year of the Putai era, while traveling to Mount Xing, he saw a cave beneath a cascading waterfall. He entered it deeply for five or six li;

emerging from the cave and traveling northeast, he discovered a stone channel where the flowing spring water was crystal clear and medicinal herbs grew in profusion. To the north of the channel were three tiled dwellings.

The pillars were extremely ancient and dilapidated; stalks of grain lay scattered across the courtyard. Inside the eastern wing were several racks of yellow volumes, with mortars and cauldrons in their midst, all covered in layers of dust.
In the western wing sat a śramaṇa, sitting upright and solemnly amidst flying dust that reached his knees.

Looking out in the four directions, there was only lush forest and hanging ravines; it was no longer a place inhabited by humans. After a short while, he encountered a divine monk whose age appeared to be...
[The man] was sixty years old. His eyebrows were about a zhang long, curling over his ears. Upon meeting him, [the Master] felt as joyful as if seeing an old friend.
When asked where he had come from, he said, "Three of us were my fellow students who have been secluding ourselves from the world here. One has gone abroad and has not yet returned;

another sits in stillness, appearing to have entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). He is currently inside the western room. Have you seen him? The Master replied, "I have already seen him. Thereupon, he took...
He pounded the grain stalks to make porridge for him. He also went into the forest to gather pears and dates for him to eat.

He asked, "What sutra do you usually recite? The Master replied, "I recite the Lotus Sutra. The monk nodded and said, "Excellent! This is a truly diligent practice. Here on the shelf in the eastern room are as many sutras as these;
would you like to hear them all recited? The Master joined his palms and said, "Yes. Thereupon, the monk [recited] throughout the entire night.

He was reciting the sutras with a clear and resonant voice. The Master was struggling with sleep, so the monk said, "Just sleep; this is my constant practice. He continued until dawn and then prepared more food for him.
When the Master thanked him and took his leave, the monk would not detain him, saying only, "A fellow student of mine is traveling away.

If you encounter him, he will bring you great awakening. It is a pity you did not meet him. With these words of farewell, he bid him adieu. The Master followed the path and returned. He then... [established... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a hagiography, likely concerning the meeting between Mazu Daoyi and Huairang before Huairang’s departure to see Nanquan.)
He went together with his companions; the location of the waterfall and the cave could not be measured.
Shi Zhi-zhan, a monk of the Northern Wei dynasty, was a native of Qi State. He resided at Xiancao Temple in the deep valley north of Mount Tai.

He simplified his affairs and spoke little; humans and birds lived there without disturbance. He recited the Lotus Sūtra, and people could not fathom his lifelong practice. When he was about to pass away, a spirit...
The monk Sengzhi said to Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, "A holy monk who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* at the Xiancao Monastery in the north will pass away today.
On that very day, the Master indeed passed away without illness; he extended one finger from each hand. A foreign monk remarked, "This is the fruit of the first stage (*prathamaphala*).
He was buried on this mountain, and later, when the tomb was opened for inspection, only his tongue remained uncorrupted. A stupa was subsequently erected to commemorate it.

Xin: During the reign of Emperor Jie-min of the Northern Wei, Lu Jingyu served as a State Academy (Guozijian) Doctor. Incriminated on charges of accumulated offenses, he was imprisoned in the city of Jinyang.

With single-minded devotion, he recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*; with his remaining strength, he also recited the entire scripture. Suddenly, his shackles and fetters fell off of their own accord. His captor...
Because he was reported at court, he was granted special clemency.
Shi Fashang of Linlü Mountain in Northern Qi was surnamed Liu and was a native of Chaoge. At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order and was known as the "Holy Śrāmaṇera.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, completing both texts in barely twenty days. He then began lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In responding to and resolving difficult objections, there were none who did not sigh in admiration and submit. Emperor Wenxuan issued an edict appointing him as the Grand Master (Dàtǒngshī).

He had the master spread his hair upon the ground and commanded the Emperor to tread upon it. People of the time said in proverbs: "Among the monastic leaders of the four seas, Daofa is supreme. This continued until the reign of Emperor Wucheng.
A person digging earth on Mount Dongshan in Bingzhou discovered an object shaped like two lips with a tongue inside, which was a vivid crimson-red color.
He reported this matter to the Emperor, who questioned various monastics, but none could identify it. The Master submitted a memorial, saying:

"This is merely the retribution for one who upholds the Lotus Sutra and whose six sense organs have not yet decayed. It is a sign of having completed a thousand recitations. Thereupon, the Emperor issued an edict to move [the object].
He prepared pure offerings and gathered those who upheld the Lotus Sūtra to surround him as he recited the scripture, entreating that a miraculous response be manifested.

As soon as he began to utter a sound, his lips and tongue vibrated in unison; all who saw this were so moved that their hair stood on end. An imperial edict was issued to seal the stone casket within a mountain chamber.

The monk Huiming of the Northern Zhou was surnamed Guo and was a native of Jinyang in Taiyuan. Possessing an exceptionally outstanding and refined spirit, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* at the age of fifteen;
in twenty-five days, he had mastered the entire text. He subsequently underwent the tonsure and ordination, specializing in the performance of the Vaipulya and Samantabhadra repentance rituals.
Later, he traveled to Xiancheng Mountain in Heyang, where he resided at Shanguang Temple. There, he lectured on the Mahāyāna and practiced dhyāna and wisdom.
There was not one who did not turn their weapons against him. Dai Kui of Jibei sent a letter to the Master, and in his reply, the Master likewise praised the secluded beauty [of the location].
The Chan Master Fayin of the same commandery was a true virtuous friend to the Master;

he went to Chan Master Neng at Guoyuan Temple in Changsha, while the fellow student Xinding had already returned to Xiancheng. One night, [the Master] took Fayin’s hand and, amidst the pine forest, [they...]

Looking back, he smiled and spoke; then, setting his will upon departing for the West, on the eleventh month of the third year of the Tianghe era of the Zhou dynasty, he sat in the full lotus posture facing west, recollecting the Buddha.
All present beheld the Buddha approaching, and with palms joined, he passed away. Extraordinary fragrances and wondrous music were heard and smelled in manifold ways.
On the eighth day of the following month, Fayin also passed away while sitting in meditation; all his miraculous signs were identical to those of the Master.
The monk Huìyuǎn of the Northern Zhou dynasty was surnamed Lǐ. A native of Dūnhuáng, he entered the monastic order at the age of thirteen and received full ordination at twenty.

He resided at Qīnghuà Temple, where a multitude of devotees flocked to him. In the second year of the Chéngguāng era, Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhou sought to suppress the Buddhist teachings; yet, while the masses remained tongue-tied, [Huìyuǎn] stood firm.

The Master resisted the imperial decree, explaining his position with utmost sincerity; his words and expression remained unyielding. He subsequently withdrew to the western mountains of Jijun, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Over the course of three years, he completed more than a thousand recitations to ensure the transmission of the remaining Dharma. In the second year of the Daxiang era, Emperor Tianyuan repented of his errors.
In both the eastern and western capitals, two temples named Zhuhu were established. The Master eventually arrived at Shaolin Temple, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* for a long time.

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, he was appointed as the Metropolitan Superintendent of Śramaṇas in Luozhou to rectify and oversee the Buddha-dharma. Whenever he gave a lecture, there was always a wild goose that would listen with docility;

it would enter the hall and crouch to listen as soon as it heard the sound of the Dharma-assembly bell, and upon the conclusion of the recitation, it would cry out and fly away. It was just like this.
For six years he remained thus, and people all marveled at him. Later, when he manifested his passing into *nirvāṇa*, there was a wondrous fragrance in his chamber.
The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai Xuchansi during the Sui Dynasty, whose posthumous name was Zhiyi, was surnamed Chen.

He was a native of Yingchuan. His mother dreamed of five-colored incense smoke swirling and entering her breast. On the evening of the child’s miraculous birth, a divine light illuminated the room. At the age of seven, he entered...
At Guoyuan Temple, he heard a monk reciting the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter). He memorized it after hearing it only once, as if it were something he had practiced in a previous life.

At the age of seventeen, he prostrated before a Buddha image and vowed to leave the household life; he felt as though he were in a dream. He saw ten thousand layers of cliffs and mountains with clouds and the sun hanging halfway down, and the vast blue sea lying deep below.
On the mountain peak was a monk who beckoned to him; in an instant, the monk extended his arm and drew the Master upward into the mountain.

He said, "Kālaṃba, you shall dwell here. At eighteen, he left the household life and went to Mount Daxian, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, the *Universal Worthy Visualization*, and others.

After twenty days, he had mastered all three sections. In the first year of the Tianjia era of the Chen dynasty, hearing that Master Zhiyi (Candrasena) was staying at Mount Dasu, he went there immediately to pay his respects.
Zhiyi said, "In the past, at Vulture Peak, we heard the *Lotus Sūtra* together."
Pursued by past affinities, he has come once more. [The Buddha] showed him the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda and expounded for him the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss.
The Master entered contemplation for fourteen days, reciting the Lotus Sūtra until he reached the "Chapter on the Medicine King": "This is true diligence;
this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. His body and mind became suddenly clear and expansive, and entering a state of tranquil concentration, he beheld Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
The assembly was solemn and had not yet dispersed when Xu Tong’s latent insights suddenly emerged. He reported what he had realized to Huisi. Nanyue sighed and said:

"Were it not for you, there would be none to realize this; were it not for me, there would be none to recognize it. The meditative state you have entered is the preliminary skillful means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*;
that which you have brought forth and sustained is the *ādi-bhrama-dhāraṇī*. Even if there were a million masters of letters, they could not exhaust your eloquence."
In the first year of the Dajian era, he arrived at Waguan Monastery in Jinling and began his lecture on the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Emperor issued an edict to suspend court for one day, ordering all his ministers to go and listen. The Master intended to rest his karmic conditions at Tiantai Mountain;

upon seeing the Southern Peak of Fulong, he lingered there with focused attention. Previously, the divine monk Dingguang had resided on this peak for thirty years. When the Master arrived, Dingguang said to him, "Have you not..."
"Do you remember the time we beckoned and led one another? Because of this, the Master realized the significance of his previous dream regarding the worship of images.

He then established a monastery on North Peak, planting pines and diverting streams so that it resembled his former vision. To the north of the temple was a separate peak named Kōtei; there he went alone to practice *dhūta* austerities.

Thereafter, the *prajñā* (wisdom) of heaven blossomed, and he extensively propagated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. As Tiantai borders the sea, the local people’s livelihoods depend on fishing; the Master...

He felt compassion for them and used the alms he had received to purchase land by the seashore to establish a pond for the release of living beings. He reported this to the Chen Emperor, who issued an edict prohibiting the capture of fish.

The Master then preached the *Guanzizai Pusa Pumenpin* (The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) Sūtra; upon hearing the Dharma, the fishermen all came to cherish life and desisted from killing.

Along the rivers and streams for over three hundred li, sixty-three locations—including Zhu, Liang, and other sites—were all transformed into sacred ponds of the Dharma. This was in the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era.

On Mount Yü-ch'uan at Chang-yang, he established a vihāra. The Martial Protector, Lord Kuan (Kuan-yin), father and son, manifested their spiritual power to request the precepts and sought to become his disciples for the protection of the Dharma.
The Master composed works such as the *Fahua xuan yi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) and served as the Great Dharma Preceptor to the two successive dynasties of Chen and Sui.
In the winter of the seventeenth year, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he commanded his attendants to chant the *Lotus Sutra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sutra*.

[Sutra]. As his final hearing and contemplation, after listening to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he offered this praise: "The Dharma-gate is the parent from which wisdom and understanding are born.
Its fundamental and manifested aspects are vast and great, subtle and wondrous, difficult to fathom. Today, I cease my chisel and snap my strings.

After listening to the *Amitāyus-sūtra*, he offered this praise: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land; yet though there are lotus ponds and jeweled trees, easy to reach, no one goes there. The fires [of hell]..."

The signs of the chariot appear; even those who are able to repent and reform shall attain rebirth there. How much more so for those who cultivate precepts and wisdom and possess the power of practicing the Way—truly, their efforts will not be in vain.
Having finished chanting the sutra, he further expounded upon the Ten Suchnesses, the Four Non-arising Principles, the Ten Dharma Realms, and the Three Contemplations.

The four immeasurables, the four *siddhāntas*, the four truths, the twelve links of dependent origination, and the six *pāramitās*—each and every dharma-gate encompasses all dharmas and enables one to penetrate the mind and reach the stage of cool serenity.
Having finished speaking, he chanted the names of the Triple Gem and entered a state like *samādhi*.
He was buried at the Fulong Cliff on Mount Tiantai, as detailed in the *Guoqing Bailu* and other biographies.

Śramaṇa Sengzhao of Hengyue Monastery during the Sui dynasty heard that the subtle and excellent practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (mind-observation) was being taught at Mount Nanyue; he traveled there specifically to pay his respects.

Whatever instructions were bestowed upon him, he understood them all completely. Later, by the command of Mount Nanyue, he practiced the *Lotus Samādhi* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*) to eliminate his long-standing karmic obstructions.
As his wondrous practice was nearing completion, he beheld the Great Being Samantabhadra riding upon a white elephant king, emitting light to bear witness to his realization.

Furthermore, he was moved by the great compassion of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), who preached the Dharma for him. Thereupon, he suddenly awakened to the profound essence of the teachings, and his eloquence became unimpeded.
Among the assembly, the Master was foremost in ascetic practices and meditative concentration.

Śramaṇa Dàshàn of Héngzhōu during the Sui dynasty dwelt among the forests and wilds from his youth. He constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and later visited Mount Nanyue, where he attained the wisdom of contemplation (*guan-hui*).
He personally practiced the *Lotus Samādhi* with such profound penetration that he eventually passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Within seven days, [the earth shook].

The heavens rained down flowers, and a wondrous fragrance coalesced. Chen Zhengye, the Magistrate of Hengyang, regularly paid him homage. He observed that Director of the Imperial Secretariat Zheng Senggao frequently praised the Master’s virtue. Once, while a hunter was surrounding a herd of deer, Senggao said to Zhengye, "You have always praised the Chan Master for his power of the Samādhi of Compassion. What will happen to these deer today? Zhengye replied, "I do not know. Senggao then said, "If you truly possess such power, why do you not manifest it now? Zhengye immediately released the deer. Later, when Zhengye went to visit the Master, he asked about the incident. The Master replied, "When the hunter surrounded the deer, I emitted a single ray of light from my hand. The deer were startled and fled; they did not even look back. Zhengye then said, "I witnessed this with my own eyes. The Master said, "It was not I who saved them. It was the power of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Zhengye further asked, "How can one obtain this Samādhi? The Master replied, "If you wish to attain it, you must first cultivate the mind of great compassion. You must regard all sentient beings as you would yourself, and never harbor thoughts of anger or resentment toward others. Zhengye subsequently practiced these teachings and attained the Way. At that time, there was a man named Wang Xuanzhi who had been suffering from a chronic illness for many years. When he heard of the Master’s reputation, he came to seek him out. The Master told him, "Your illness is severe; you should go to the riverbank and recite the *Heart Sūtra*. Xuanzhi followed his instructions. After seven days, he felt a sudden change and recovered completely. His wife, Lady Zhang, was also afflicted by a chronic ailment. She too went to the riverbank and recited the sūtra. After three days, she was cured. Both husband and wife then became lay disciples of the Master. There was also a certain Liang Daoyu, who was a man of great wealth and influence. He once invited the Master to his residence and provided him with every necessity. One day, Daoyu asked the Master, "I have heard that you can transform gold and silver into earth and stone. Is this true? The Master replied, "I am indeed capable of doing so. Daoyu then said, "If you can do this, please turn my gold and silver into earth and stone. The Master laughed and said, "Why would I do such a thing? I am merely a man of humble virtue. How could I possibly perform such a feat? Daoyu pressed him repeatedly. The Master finally said, "If you insist, I shall do it. He then took some gold and silver and placed them on a table. With a snap of his fingers, he transformed them into earth and stone. Daoyu was astonished and deeply moved. He then offered the Master vast amounts of wealth and property, but the Master declined them all. He only accepted a small amount of grain to support himself. Later, Daoyu fell ill and died. His son, Liang Zhongxian, inherited his father’s estate. Zhongxian was a man of great talent and learning, and he held the Master in high esteem. He often visited him and sought instruction. One day, Zhongxian asked the Master, "My late father was very fond of you. Why did you not accept his offerings? The Master replied, "His offerings were excessive. I feared that if I accepted them, I would become attached to worldly things and lose my spiritual focus. Therefore, I declined them. Zhongxian then said, "If you had accepted them, your family would have been well-provided for. Now we are left in poverty. The Master said, "Poverty is not a hardship for one who has attained the Way. Wealth and status are but fleeting illusions. Do not let the affairs of the world disturb your mind. Zhongxian bowed in gratitude and departed. The Master remained in seclusion, practicing the Way with unwavering resolve. His fame spread far and wide, and people from all quarters came to seek his guidance. Those who encountered him were invariably transformed by his compassionate power. Thus, the Master’s legacy endured, and his influence reached across the land. His life came to an end at the age of eighty-four, having fulfilled his mission of benefiting sentient beings. His remains were interred at Mount Lu, where his spirit continues to inspire generations of practitioners. This concludes the account of the Master’s life and deeds.
