Jiye immediately led his attendants, and they all chanted "Namo to the Great and Virtuous Meditation Master" in unison. The herd of deer leaped into the air and departed;
the entire assembly was struck with awe and admiration.

Shi Huicheng of Jingzhou during the Sui dynasty was surnamed Duan of Linyang; he could recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, and others by heart.
After the sutra had been recited, he met the Great Meditation Master Si of Mount Nanyue, who instructed him to enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

He practiced according to these instructions for three years, whereupon demonic activities and meditation-ghosts were suddenly and completely dispersed. Later, he went to Zhiyang and established Chanhui Temple.

During the sixth month, when the river was in flood, he obtained a beam of timber one night. A man named Duanhong, who served as the temple’s caretaker, suddenly lost consciousness; when the Master arrived, he revived.
He said: "At first, when he was captured and brought before the king, the Master saw him ascending the hall and said, 'This man's merit is not yet exhausted; I pray that you grant him clemency.

The king rose and prostrated at his feet, and as the Master had spoken, the man was released. Furthermore, there was Vinaya Master Chang, who one midnight felt for a louse and threw it to the ground."
When dawn arrived, the Master said, "Last night a lay devotee was suffering from the cold; it was truly pitiful. Chang was deeply ashamed and took this as a lifelong warning.
Shi Huichao of Wuzhen Temple on Mount Zhongnan during the Sui dynasty was surnamed Shen of Danyang. From childhood he followed the Buddhist path and specialized in recitation.
Fahua heard that Master Sida of Guangzhou had attained solitary awakening to the One Vehicle and profoundly understood the Three Contemplations.

He then, with a humble mind and purified self, followed Master Zhiyi as his disciple to request instruction. Sida remarked, "He has transcended the divine treasury; he is one who has attained the stage of patience.
Later, when traveling to Mount Heng, Fahua again traveled by the same path as Zhiyi, reciting the sutras for years. Subsequently, he withdrew to Zhongnan Mountain, where he practiced for eight years.

Dao, having fallen ill for a short time, summoned the assembly and told them: "Coming and going are the constant nature of things. I do not rejoice in long life, nor do I grieve at death at nightfall.
The emptiness of the primary truth and the contemplation of pure wisdom are my staff. Having said this, he passed away facing west.
The Master entered the Way at the age of nine and immediately began reciting the Lotus Sutra. Over fifty years, he recited it more than ten thousand times.
His spiritual responses and auspicious signs were too numerous to recount.

The Sui dynasty monk Shi Huíwēi was a native of Jānglíng. In his youth, he relied upon Mount Nányuè to practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and devoted himself to contemplating profound stillness.
He subsequently attained the *dhāraṇī* for understanding the languages of all sentient beings; whenever he heard the sounds of humans, domestic animals, or birds, he immediately knew their meaning.
Later, he further manifested supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), flying through the air and walking upon water as if treading on level ground. His secret practices were extraordinary.
No one was able to fathom him.

Shi Guanding of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Sui dynasty was surnamed Wu. A native of Zhang’an in Linhai, he was able to recite the names of the Triple Gem following his mother when he was only three months old.
At the age of seven, he left the secular life; he memorized ten thousand words a day and received full ordination at twenty. He then went to pay his respects...
The Wise One (Zhìzhě) received and practiced the methods of contemplation; after long and diligent study, he was suddenly granted formal certification (*kṣānti*).

Later, he followed Zhìzhě to Guangzhai Temple in Jinling to listen to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Furthermore, at Yùquán in Jiangling, he received the *Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* (*Fahua xuanyi*) and the *Treatise on Contemplation and Practice* (*Zhiguan*).
In his later years, he resided at Chēngxīn Jíngshè in Kuàijī, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*. At that time, there were those such as Kūa Lǎng and Lóng Jī who surpassed [all others].
Yunmai was impressed by his words. On the eighth month of the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away; a wondrous fragrance filled his chamber.

The Master’s transformation spread through the mundane world, and his spiritual efficacy was boundless. Whenever he recited the sutras or sat in meditation, heavenly flowers would often drift down beside him.
A villager named Yufa Long lived thirty li from the mountain; afflicted by illness, he was on the verge of death. His son rushed there to pray for his salvation. The Master...
To propagate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he burned sandalwood incense. When a sick person smelled the fragrance entering their nostrils from afar, they were healed immediately.
Furthermore, he took pleasure in the southern ridges of Nanling, at a place called Anzhou, where emerald trees and clear streams flowed with hidden springs, making it impassable for human paths.
The Master lingered there, cherishing its beauty, and looking back at the site, he vowed: "If this land should become level and open, I shall surely return here."
He preached the sutras; before even ten days had passed, white sand surged forth everywhere until the ground was as level as a jade mirror.
He then preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* to repay this spiritual grace.
Shi Zhi-guan of the Nantianzhu Monastery at Lingyin during the Sui dynasty was a member of the Fan clan of Qiantang. From his youth, he possessed extraordinary features:
his tongue was purple with a rosette pattern, and the characters for "immortal" (*xianren*) were visible on both his palms. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* at a rate of one fascicle per day.

In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, during a severe drought, he was invited to lecture on the *Sūtra of the Sea Dragon King*. Once the introduction to the king [of the sūtra] had concluded, torrential rain poured down. The district...

Regarding Mount Xilingyin: formerly known as Xianju, after the Master had practiced *dhūta* in a stone chamber, the community constructed a vihāra for him, naming it Nantianzhu, and invited him to reside there.
He constantly lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his essential practice. Whenever he washed his hands, the droplets that fell [were preserved].

The ground did not become damp; everyone marveled at this. One day, the deity of Gaotingshan requested that he lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Moved by this, the deity offered up his residence to be converted into a monastery.

During the Sui dynasty, there was the Tiantai monk Shi Puming, whose original name was Fajing. He was of the Zhu family of Kuaiji. From childhood, he would join his palms and recite [the Buddha’s name].
The Buddha. Suddenly, a monk pointed him toward Tiantai, saying, "There is an *ādikarmika-bodhisattva* there who preaches the Dharma to transform the world.
In the fourteenth year of the Daye era, he traveled to Mount Tai to serve Zhiyi, where he specialized in the practice of the *chánfǎ* (repentance rites) and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* daily.

Later, he followed [Zhiyi] to Mount Lu, where at Tao Kan’s Shrine of the Auspicious Image, he performed the *Qing Guanyin Samādhi*. While in the midst of the formal practice, a voice was heard from within the shrine.
Moved by this, a strange monk changed his name to Puming (Universal Radiance), and Zhiyi subsequently followed him. Later, he returned to Guoqing Temple.
As the place where he resided was far from water, the Master pointed to a rock and said, "Would it not be delightful if a spring flowed from this rock?
Immediately, the spring gushed forth, providing for a thousand people every day; this is the present-day Xizhangquan (Staff-Holder Spring).

Shi Zhiyuan of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty was surnamed Zheng and hailed from Nanyang. Having left secular life at a young age, he traveled to various regions to seek the Way.
Upon arriving in Jinling, he met Zhizhe, to whom he paid homage as his teacher and requested instruction; Zhizhe secretly transmitted to him the essential points of the mind.

When Zhizhe later returned to Mount Tai, he entrusted the entire assembly to Zhiyuan’s care. For twenty years, he guided his students with steady and skillful exhortation, and they all turned their hearts toward him. Such was the Master’s life.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than ten thousand times. In the place where he resided, the water in his pitcher would spontaneously fill itself.
In the twelfth year of the Daye era, he passed away lying on his right side; celestial flowers rained down, and the entire region was shrouded in darkness.
The Sui dynasty monk Zhizao was of the Zhang clan from Linhai. At the age of twenty, he ascended Mount Tiantai to attend upon Great Master Zhiyi, seeking to leave the household life.
Zhiyi instructed him to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* while concurrently practicing samādhi.

On the night of the fourteenth day of the second month, after his repentance rites were completed, he saw a nine-headed dragon emerge from the earth and ascend into the void. When Tianming asked about this vision, Zhiyi said: "This signifies..."
Sentient beings of the nine realms who hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* will, in future ages, shatter ignorance and enter the emptiness of the Dharma-nature.

Later, he moved his residence to Baolin Monastery and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Samādhi*. During the first watch of the night, spirits immediately shook the door panels;
for twenty-one days, this occurred every night, eventually leading them to strike the pillars, break through the walls, extinguish the lamps, and manifest their forms before the Master.

He remained entirely unmoved, engaging only in seated meditation and the recitation of sutras. When the third seven-day period concluded, he saw a youth dressed in blue robes who praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Having spoken, the youth vanished.
The Sui dynasty monk Zhixi was of the Chen clan from Yingchuan. Having left secular life in his childhood, he went to Mount Tiantai to receive the instructions on dhyāna from the Great Master Zhiyi.
He further cultivated meditative concentration and resided constantly at the Chan practice hall on Fulong Peak to practice the Lotus Samādhi.

At that time, he wished to construct an incense altar; however, the timber on Xianglu Peak was exceptionally beautiful and unique, and the Master desired to clear it for use. The assembly, however, maintained that the site was occupied by a deity.
He was filled with doubt. That night, he dreamed that a deity sent him a message, saying: "The cypress and juniper trees on Incense Burner Peak shall all be surrendered for the sutra platform;

you may cut them down. He subsequently felled them. There was a monk named Fayun who wished to go to the summit of the peak to practice seated meditation. The Master stopped him, saying, "Your spiritual power is weak, and the mountain deities there are fierce and violent;
it is not appropriate for you to go. Yun did not comply. After only one night had passed, the deity manifested his form and drove him back.
Only then did he realize the former meaning and develop a profound sense of reverence. The Master once went to the Jewel Stūpa of King Aśoka and performed eighty-four thousand prostrations.
In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he sat upright in the full lotus posture, still holding a *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) while preaching the Dharma.
When his disciples asked where he would be reborn, he replied, "As I see in my dream, it shall be in Tuṣita. He remained solemnly as if entering meditative absorption, and passed away into emptiness.
Within it, there was the sound of stringed and wind instruments; after a long while, it ceased.
Shi Faxiang of Zhengjian Temple in Yangzhou during the Sui dynasty was a member of the Li clan of Wei-yang.

He entered the monastic order and practiced with rigorous austerity, studying under Zhiyi and specializing in the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra. Beside Qixia Temple on Mount She, he established the Lotus Hall and performed the Samādhi Repentance.
The Master practiced the Dharma with diligent effort for twenty-one days and attained great spiritual omens; yet he remained silent and did not speak.

Wild tigers were causing havoc in the mountains, so the assembly prepared a great vegetarian feast to avert the calamity. Suddenly, a tiger entered the midst of the crowd and seized a person, carrying him away. The Master called out in a loud voice:
"Today I have specifically prepared this vegetarian feast for you; you may release this man. The tiger immediately set the man down and withdrew.

Shortly thereafter, several dozen tigers gathered in great numbers at the site of the feast. The crowd was terrified and fled, but the Master struck the necks of the tigers with his staff and preached the Dharma to them.
Thereafter, he retreated into seclusion, leaving no trace of his whereabouts.

During the Sui dynasty, the monk Dengguan was of the Sun clan of Fuyang; he received the practice of *citta-vipaśyanā* from Zhiyi and resided at Tiantai Mountain, where he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
During the Zhenguan era, he traveled to Yuhang and preached the Dharma while seated upon a platform at Farin Temple. On the first day of the New Year, there appeared a person dressed in royal attire.

When he arrived, it was said that the deity of Gaotingshan had come to pay his respects and inquire about receiving the precepts of the Dharma. The Master immediately requested an incense burner and lit incense, bestowing upon him the Bodhisattva Great Precepts.
The deity then expressed his gratitude with prostrations and withdrew.
Shi Dazhi of Fulin Temple on Mount Lu during the Sui dynasty was a member of the Gu clan of Kuaiji. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven and took Master Zhizhe of Tiantai as his teacher.
In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, he traveled to Mount Lu and resided at Huading Temple, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The environment was desolate and tranquil; his voice was clear and melodic, and everyone delighted in hearing him. Later, he established a place for silent contemplation before the summit of Mount Ganlu.

At the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa), he took the dhūta ascetic practices as his vocation. Standing alone and solitary, he did not avoid roaring tigers; he would frequently cast himself before them to feed them, yet the tigers would always retreat.

He was Shi Daoyue of Qingxi Mountain in Jingzhou during the Sui dynasty, born into the Zhang family of Zhaoqiu. He left the household life at Yuquan Temple, where his capacity and insight were profound.
Profound and serene, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* constantly. When Master Zhi first entered Yuquan, there were no bells or chimes;

he obtained a piece of extraordinary stone from the spring source, hung it up, and struck it. Its resonance was clear and penetrating. Whenever the Master recited the sūtra, his voice was like the sound of a clear stream flowing with refined melody;
he would complete an entire fascicle before striking the chime once. Those who heard it were struck with solemn reverence. He often ate while walking in the shadows, always leaving behind...

A portion [of these offerings] was used to provide for those who fly and swim. Influenced by his benevolence and compassion, some birds would alight upon his shoulders, while others would float and flutter in his hands;
such auspicious responses were manifold.
Shi Tanxun, of the Sui dynasty, resided at Bajian Mountain Temple in Huaizhou. His secular surname was Yang, and he was a native of Huayin. He entered the monastic order on Mount Bailu.

He devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Having heard that Master Chou of Yunmen Temple on Longshan was a master of the mountain-like stillness and the river-like clarity, whose skill as a craftsman had been peerless for ages, he immediately paid his respects from afar.
Later, he moved to reside at Lutu Valley to practice meditation, whereupon a dried-up spring gushed forth once more and deer began to roam the precincts.
At one time, while traveling to Yunmen to lecture on the Dharma, he encountered a path shrouded in thick mist; thereupon, he was moved by the mountain deity to [act on his behalf].

He pointed out the way for them. Furthermore, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered two tigers fighting; they would not cease for many hours. The Master took up his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) to separate them and used his own body as a shield.

The tigers lowered their heads and dispersed. Whenever he entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he would remain for a period of seven days. During the Kaihuang era, he was granted an imperial letter of commendation for his extraordinary virtues.
Shi Tanyun of Weizhou during the Sui dynasty was a native of Dingzhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth and constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He traveled extensively across Mount Wutai, where he witnessed numerous miraculous manifestations. He stayed at Pomegranate Tree Temple (*Moguosi*) on the Northern Terrace for over twenty years, never ceasing his practice of meditation and recitation.

Amidst the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, when he was already seventy years old, he went into seclusion on Mount Bigan. There, continuing his practice day and night, he restrained his mind without slackening; he frequently desired to transcribe [the scriptures].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* had not been completed for several years. As his long-accumulated vow reached its fulfillment, a scholar suddenly arrived and said, "I am skilled at copying scriptures.

I wish to fulfill your master's aspiration. Thereupon, he swept the room and smeared the floor with mud. Holding incense in his mouth, he wrote in silence; emerging from the room to wash his hands and returning to bathe himself, within less than ten days, all seven fascicles were finished.
He was about to offer them as a religious gift (*dakṣiṇā*), but in an instant they vanished. Later, when barbarian raiders suddenly arrived, [he] concealed them...

The scripture had been in a rock cave for many years; though the region was peaceful and free of bandits, the scripture could not be found. It was eventually discovered among the grass at the foot of the cliff.

Although both the outer box and the inner cloth were completely rotted away, the color of the scrolls remained as it was when new. In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, Vinaya Master Xuan personally witnessed this event.
Shi Huikai of Anle Temple in Jiangdu during the Sui dynasty was born into the Zhang clan of Qinghe. Having entered the path in his childhood, he made the Pure Land his goal.
Through the power of his single-minded devotion, he moved the divine: suddenly, a monk from Qizhou named Daoquan arrived, carrying an image of Amitāyus Buddha.

Exquisite and subtle in its craftsmanship, it was said to be the work of a Bodhisattva possessing the five supernatural powers from the Kukkutārāma Monastery in India, who traveled through the air to that World of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) to paint the sacred image. Having thus fulfilled his long-held aspiration, he felt profound reverence;
then, beholding a divine light shining brilliantly, he rejoiced at such a rare occurrence. In the fifth month of the fifth year of the Daye era, suddenly [the face]...
After completing his prostrations toward the west, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. The Master practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* with increasing devotion as he grew older.
He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* fifty times and, while propagating the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, he vowed his heart to the Pure Land; he was the foremost figure of his time.
During the Sui dynasty, Shi Huigong of Zhaoti Monastery in Yizhou entered into a spiritual covenant with his fellow student, the monk Huiyuan.

Later, they traveled to Jingzhou and Yangzhou to seek the Way before returning home. They were separated for thirty years. During a night conversation, Huiyuan’s speech flowed like a stream, while the Master remained silent and offered no reply.
Huiyuan asked, "Does the Honorable One have nothing to attain? The Master replied, "My nature is dark and I possess no understanding. Huiyuan said, "Is this not [the case]?"
"Have you recited any sutras? The Master replied, "I have only recited one scroll of the 'Universal Gate' chapter of the *Lotus Sutra*.

I shall recite it for you; simply listen with a sincere heart. He then established a ritual altar and ascended the high seat. As he first raised his voice to chant the title of the sutra, they perceived a fragrant aroma.

After a while, celestial music was heard shaking the void, and flowers rained down in profusion. Only when the recitation was finished did these phenomena cease. Dao Yuan paid him respectful obeisance and expressed his gratitude.
Shi Fachong of the Sui dynasty was a member of the Bi clan of Jiushang. He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra and was also well-versed in the Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra.

Residing at Huacheng Monastery on Mount Lu, he frequently exhorted the monastic community not to allow women to enter the temple, as doing so would undermine the Buddha’s transformative influence above and degrade the local customs below.

At first, there were those among the assembly who did not follow her. The Master then threw herself down from Mount Xianglu at the summit of the mountain, vowing to crush her body and bones to be reborn in a Pure Land.
Suddenly, while in mid-air, her head turned upward and she descended slowly; her body suffered no injury whatsoever.
The assembly was moved by this marvel and began to strictly prohibit women from entering. At the end of the Kaihuang era, she passed away while seated in meditation during the height of summer.
A putrid odor arose, yet a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
Shi Falang of the Sui dynasty, surnamed Xu, was a native of Nanyang. He had no fixed place of residence and mostly stayed in Ezhou.

At that time, he was reciting various sutras, but his aspiration was focused exclusively on the Lotus Sutra. He made a solemn vow to recite it, completing seven repetitions in a single sitting. After a long while, his voice resounded like thunder.
His voice resonated clearly at both near and far distances, and the world consequently named him Fahualang (Lamp of the Lotus Sūtra). There was a bhikṣuṇī who had been possessed by a ghost;
she attained profound insight and understanding, such that everyone praised her for her intelligence. The Master said, "This is a malevolent ghost," and he rebuked it with a stern voice.
The demon immediately fled in terror, and [the bhikṣuṇī] was suddenly restored as if nothing had happened.
Shi Faxi of Yongzhou during the Sui dynasty was born into the Li family of Xiangyang. At the age of seven, he left the secular life with the resolve to uphold the *Lotus Sūtra*.
During the Renshou era, he resided at Chanding Temple in the capital. Desiring to pray for spiritual inspiration through the unseen, he vowed to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* one thousand times.

Consequently, he did not remain in his usual quarters but instead wandered about the temple chanting the scripture. When the count reached eight hundred, his vow remained undistracted; suddenly, the monks of the same monastery saw him.

There was a jeweled carriage and a necklace. He entered the master’s room and examined them closely, yet found nothing at all; only then did he realize it was a response to his profound spiritual resonance.
Shi Facheng of Wuzhen Temple on Mount Zhongnan during the Sui dynasty was of the Fan clan from Yongzhou. He resided at Wangxiao Temple in Lantian.

He devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and traveled across famous mountains carrying his book-cases. Resolving to practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, he dreamed that Samantabhadra exhorted him to transcribe the Mahāyāna scriptures;

he then commissioned artisans to copy the eight sections of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, he constructed a hall for the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and, with utmost diligence, transcribed, received, and upheld it.
At that time, the Master of Literature Zhang Jing, who was already skilled in calligraphy from youth, invited him to [his residence].
In his mountain retreat, he incensed himself with fragrance and transcribed the entire collection. At that time, a strange bird was moved to fly to his sutra desk, where it naturally became tame.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, while he was hand-copying the *Lotus Sūtra* on an open clearing, he had to leave for other business and did not secure the work. He encountered a torrential downpour;
when he hurried back to observe it, the entire desk was dry, while the rest of the area was flooded with water. In the summer of the fourteenth year, he spoke to his attendants...
The man said, "I have heard that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and that birth and extinction do not abide. That the nine grades of rebirth exist has now been proven true.
Now there is a youth to welcome me; I shall depart from this world. Having spoken, light issued from his mouth, illuminating the interior of the pillar.

Furthermore, a rare and fragrant incense was smelled as he sat upright and passed away. He had recited and studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for approximately ten years, totaling more than ten thousand recitations.

During the Sui dynasty, the monk Fa’an resided at Jianyuan Temple; he was profoundly versed in the profound essentials [of the teachings] and constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, delivering lectures on it more than forty times.
Suddenly, at the four corners of the lecture seat, clusters of flowers sprang up, numbering more than ten stalks, with colors alternating between yellow and white;
they resembled lotuses, radiating fragrance and light. After another ten days, eight or nine more flowers appeared beside the lecturer’s platform and where the assembly sat;
they only withered after a month. Monastics and laypeople gathered to observe them, marveling at this rare and auspicious portent.

The Sui dynasty monk Fatai was a native of Longshan in Meizhou. He constantly recited the Lotus Sūtra and had personally transcribed a copy of the scripture, which frequently manifested miraculous signs.
While traveling toward Yizhou to have it bound and displayed, the scroll suddenly fell into the waters of Ze Bridge. Unable to find it, the Master wept in sorrow.
While walking up and down the shore, he suddenly saw a bundle upon a small island. He ordered it to be retrieved; it was a scripture.

Grasses and trees had supported it, so that not a single spot was damp. The Master was filled with boundless joy. He then proceeded to Chengdu, where he completed the binding of the text using sandalwood rollers, making it most magnificent.
He returned it to his home temple, where every night a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber. The Master diligently maintained its recitation.
He would certainly recite it once every night. At that time, there was Dharma Master Biao lecturing on the sutras at that temple.
One evening, he went to the place where the Master was reciting the sutras and saw a great multitude of people kneeling with their palms joined; Biao broke into a sweat and withdrew.
Śramaṇa Xuànxiù of Jìhuá Temple in Huángzhōu during the Sui dynasty constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, and it was always accompanied by extraordinary signs.

Once, during the height of the summer heat, while the Master was in the midst of his recitation, the temple monks saw a solemn and imposing retinue of guards surrounding him. Terrified, they informed their companions, who all went together to observe as before;
looking up into the air, they saw it filled to the horizon without end. The fourfold assembly all marveled at this divine marvel.
The Sui dynasty monk Xingjian constantly practiced meditative contemplation and was renowned for his strict integrity. Once traveling east, his route led through Mount Tai;

he stayed overnight at a temple on the mountain. The temple priest said, "Those who have recently stayed here have mostly met with calamity and violence; you must not do so. The Master did not listen.
He then took refuge beneath the eaves of the hall, sitting upright to recite the sutras. After about one watch of the night, he heard the sound of tinkling jade ornaments within the room.

In a short while, a deity emerged, his robes and cap most magnificent, with a brilliant retinue surrounding him. He joined his palms toward the Master, who invited him to sit and engage in conversation.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal, the Master asked, "It is said by popular tradition that Mount Tai governs the ghosts; is this truly so? The spirit replied, "It is.
[The Master continued,] "Do you wish for me to see those who have passed away? The Master said, "There were two fellow monks who died; I wish to see them. The spirit asked their names.
He then said, "One has already been born into the human world, and the other is in prison undergoing judgment; they cannot be summoned."
"Come; you may come to see the Master. They immediately rose together and went to a certain place, where they saw the flames of hell blazing most fiercely.
The messenger led the Master in, and from afar he saw a person within the fire wailing and crying out; the stench of their scorched flesh and blood was so unbearable that he could not bear to look.
The Master piteously requested to leave, but the spirit sat with him as before. The Master asked, "May I rescue my fellow practitioners? The spirit replied, "It can be done.

If you can transcribe the *Lotus Sūtra*, they will surely be able to escape. As dawn approached, the spirit took its leave and entered the shrine. The temple priest, seeing that the Master had not died, found it strange.

After the Master departed, he hurriedly reported on his previous vow. Once the transcription and binding of the scripture were complete, he took it with him to stay overnight at the temple; the spirit emerged once more.
As before, he joyfully prostrated and said, "I have already learned that my teacher has transcribed this scripture.
Now that he has begun writing the title of the sutra, I have been liberated from [the underworld] and am now born among humans. This was an event that occurred during the Daye era.
Lu Chun of Wu Commandery was a lay devotee of the Sui dynasty. His heart constantly aspired to the Way, and he recited and upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* day and night.

Later, he suddenly fell ill; lying on his back, he gazed at the ceiling without blinking for even a moment. When a monk who was a spiritual friend came to inquire after his illness, he asked him, "Why are you looking up at the rafters?
He replied, "The Buddha has prophesied that Lu Chun shall be reborn in the Yāma Heaven; now I see it."
The celestial palaces, city towers, and the various hosts of devas gazed upon him with tireless devotion.

During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Yan Gong, a man from Jiangzhou, had throughout his life maintained a pure mind and taken refuge in the Dharma. He constructed a vihāra outside the city walls and transcribed the Lotus Sūtra, making pure offerings to it.
He ensured that the paper, brushes, and ink used for the transcription were all of the highest quality, approaching the task with sincere faith.
He practiced generosity and refrained from deception. He managed his affairs according to what he obtained, never soliciting anything.

Whenever he finished a scroll, he would invariably personally verify every character, enduring this for a long time without weariness. Once, someone requested ten thousand coins for the sake of sutras; Hui-gong, having no choice, gave them to him.
The borrower’s boat capsized, spilling water and losing the money, though he barely escaped with his life. On that very day, Hui-gong entered his household treasury.

He saw that the money he had borrowed was there, damp as if it had been washed with water. Later, upon hearing of this matter, he realized it was a supernatural marvel. Wang Fanxing of Linyi during the Sui dynasty was blind from childhood.

Out of compassionate concern, his mother orally transmitted the *Lotus Sūtra* to him. Clad in coarse cloth and subsisting on simple vegetarian food, he never faltered in his meditation and recitation;
in total, he recited the sūtra seventeen thousand times. Later, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture, leaving behind these final words:
Her corpse was exposed in a wilderness charnel ground. After a long time, her skin and flesh had completely decayed, yet her tongue alone remained uncorrupted, its color like that of a lotus flower.

During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Cui Yanwu of Boling, the Prefectural Governor of Wei Province, while on an inspection tour of a certain district, said to his attendants, "In a previous life, I was a woman in this district; I now wish to go and see her. Thereupon, he mounted his horse.
He entered Xiuxiang Lane and arrived at the house. He ordered the door to be knocked, and an elderly man came out to receive him.

Yanwu ascended the hall and, looking toward a high spot on the eastern wall, said to the host, "In the past, the Lotus Sutra I stored here, along with five gold hairpins, were kept in this very place."

At the end of the seventh fascicle of the sutra, several lines of text had been lost due to fire damage. Whenever he recited the scripture to this point, his heart felt as though something were missing.
He ordered his attendants to break through the wall to retrieve it, and they found it exactly as he had said. The owner wept uncontrollably;
Yǎnwǔ presented him with generous gifts before departing.
Daoxuan, the Vinaya Master of Ximing Monastery in Jingzhao during the Tang dynasty, was a native of Huzhou. He was the son of Jian Shen, who served as the Minister of Personnel under the Sui dynasty.
When his mother was pregnant with him, she dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said, "The one you carry in your womb is the Vinaya Master Sengyou.

At the age of sixteen, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, completing it in twenty days. During the Wude era, he lived in seclusion at Zhongnan Mountain. His dwelling lacked water, and a divine being appeared.
He pointed to a spot on the ground, and when they dug more than a foot deep, a spring gushed forth spontaneously; it was named Baekchon-sa (White Spring Temple). Later, he moved to Pongdeok-sa.

While practicing the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (般舟定), he was moved by a multitude of dragons who came to pay their respects and offered him rare flowers and fruits. The Master’s monastic virtue was peerless;

he composed the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo*), as well as the *Record of Inner Scriptures*, the *Record of Miraculous Responses of the Triple Gem*, the *Extended Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism*, and the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Biography. During the Zhenguan era, while [the Master] was secluded in Yunshi Mountain, people saw a celestial youth attending to his side.

While performing the night walking meditation (yinxingdao) at Ximing Temple, the Master stumbled and fell against the steps. A youth clad in armor supported him; the Master asked, "What deity are you?
He replied, "I am Nanda, the prince of Vaiśravaṇa. Because your precepts and virtue are sublime and profound, I have come to provide protection."

The Master then inquired extensively about matters concerning the Buddha-dharma, and the deity recounted each point to him. The deity bestowed upon the Master a Buddha-tooth relic along with a precious hand, as tokens of faith, and then vanished.
In the spring of the second year of the Qianfeng era, he was moved by the arrival of a celestial being who spoke with him regarding the characteristics of the Vinaya.
One day, another celestial being came to pay his respects and said, "Master Vinayadhara, you shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. He presented a volume of texts and departed.
This was the Incense of the Thorny Forest. On the third day of the tenth month, he passed away while sitting in meditation. He was titled the Master Chengzhao, the Founder of Nanshan.

When the Master composed the Preface to the Lotus Sutra, the Heavenly Lord Wei declared that because the Lotus Sutra is most venerable and supreme, it would not be easy to provide a preeminent introduction;

he therefore reported this to the Buddhas of the ten directions, all of whom gave their approval. The preface was then first transmitted; this is the very "Preface to the Widely Disseminated [Sutra]" used today.
The Tang dynasty monk Jizang was surnamed An. His ancestors were originally from Parthia (Anxi), and his family had moved to Nanhai many generations prior.
He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and later received full ordination. His aspiration was to transmit the lamp of the Dharma, causing the wheel of the Dharma to turn in succession.

He resided at Riyen Temple in the capital, where he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Those who came to hear his teachings numbered in the tens of thousands. At the beginning of the Daye era, he transcribed one thousand copies of the *Lotus Sūtra* and further established [a separate collection].

Facing an image of Samantabhadra, he personally sat in meditation and contemplated the principle of the true nature (*dharmatā*). In the sixth year of the Wude era, he moved his residence to Yanxing Temple, where offerings from various quarters arrived in abundance.
One clear morning, he burned incense, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away. As it was the height of summer, his complexion remained exceptionally fresh and white.
He was interred within a stone crypt on the northern cliff. Throughout his life, the Master had lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* more than thirty times. Just as he was about to...
The *Treatise on Not Fearing Death at the End of Life* states: "Death originates from birth; one ought to weep for birth, rather than fear death.
The full text is not recorded here due to its length.
The Tang dynasty monk Huizhu, surnamed Jia of Shizhou, first arrived at Gānlù Temple in the capital to receive full ordination, where he specialized in reciting the Dharma.
Huā was moved by the mountain deity to provide offerings for him. As he practiced the Way during the six periods of the day, birds and beasts followed his path as if listening with reverence.

He further conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon those in both the hidden and manifest realms. During the Wǔdé era, he resided at Xiānglín Monastery. At that time, the Duke of Língyáng was serving as the Governor of Yìzhōu.
He brought more than a hundred pack-animals into the monastery and stationed them in the lecture hall; none dared to disobey.

When the Master saw the filth and disorder, he immediately entered his quarters, took up his mendicant’s staff and the three robes, and went out. He raised the staff toward the donkeys and mules, and they all fell prostrate at once.

The local officials were greatly alarmed and seized the Master to submit a formal report. Lingyang was not at all surprised, but simply said, "I am deeply grateful that the Master has broken my stinginess."
For his great benefit, [the Emperor] presented him with ten *jin* of agarwood. After returning to the capital, [the Emperor] received the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
The monk Xuanzang of Da Ci’en Monastery in the Tang capital was surnamed Chen. A native of Chenliu, he was able to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* by the age of eleven.
He was exceptionally upright and sincere. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, he traveled to the Western Regions to retrieve sūtras not yet available in China. Upon his arrival...

In the kingdom of Kuśa, [the Master] crossed the Gaṅgā River with several merchants. According to the customs of that country, human sacrifice was offered to the gods; they were about to execute the Master to use him as an offering.
Suddenly, a great wind arose, and dust and sand rose to fill the sky, causing the daylight to turn dark and gloomy. The multitude there took the Master to be a holy man.
He was subsequently released and traveled to Central India, where he heard the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Upon entering the city of Rājagṛha, he studied under the master Śīlabhadra of the Ūrdhvamśa school, exhaustively investigating the secret depths of the Mahāyāna and daily increasing his realization of wisdom.

In total, he visited more than one hundred and fifty countries over a period of nineteen years. He then brought back scriptures and images to the capital, where he later translated seventy-five works, including both sutras and śāstras.
In the second month of the first year of the Linde era, he took leave of the assembly and instructed his attendants to recite the name of Maitreya Tathāgata.

Lying on his right side, he passed away. A monk of extraordinary appearance offered incense and anointed the Master’s body. By imperial decree, following the precedent of the World-Honored One, he was interred in a stupa on the northern plain of Fanchuan.
Śramaṇa Xuánwǎn of Puguāng Monastery in the capital of the Táng dynasty was surnamed Yáng; he was a native of Huáyīn.

He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Mahāyāna scriptures, and other texts, thoroughly investigating their profound principles and exquisitely elucidating their subtle mysteries. In the second year of the Rénshòu era, he commissioned a sixteen-foot golden image of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
His utmost sincerity moved the unseen realm, and the heavens rained down wondrous flowers that drifted like mica. That night, the sky...

His practice continued until dawn before he would cease. Every eighth day of the second month, during his period of observing the precepts, he would purify himself through fasting and perform the Way according to the rites of the twenty-five Buddhas and the Thousand-Turn Mantra.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor commanded the Crown Prince and the various princes to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts from him as their teacher.
Xiao Yu, the Vice President of the Left, and his brothers frequently consulted him regarding the principle of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s teaching that the three vehicles are one.

The Master analyzed [the teachings] for him, repeating them again and again until he was weary. Du Ruhui, the Right Vice-Director, left a final testament expressing his wish to become a disciple through successive kalpas.

Every time the Master conferred the precepts or preached the Dharma, shamans and diviners would suddenly report seeing various classes of spirits and ghosts gathering from all directions, as if they were receiving instructions.

Śramaṇa Kuiji of the Great Ci’en Monastery of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wei-chi. A native of Chang’an, he was a disciple of Master Xuanzang and was thoroughly versed in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he stayed overnight in an ancient temple by the West River. There he saw a scroll of scripture emitting light;

upon unrolling it, he discovered the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Rebirth Above*. He then took up his brush to compose a commentary, and from the tip of his pen, he obtained fourteen grains of śarīra, which were red in color.
Yun was lovely to behold; his countenance was stately and his heart compassionate. He traveled everywhere to transform and guide others.

Reaching Boling in the east, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and concurrently composed a great commentary (*mahā-ṭīkā*) upon it. He once fashioned a statue of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva made of jade and transcribed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in golden characters;
both emitted divine light that filled the chamber with a brilliant radiance. Initially, Master Xuanzang had personally transmitted to him the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
The Master fully grasped its subtle essence and was hailed throughout the land as the Dharma Master Ci'en.

At that time, Vinaya Master Xuan, who had moved the heavens by his propagation of the precepts, received daily offerings from the celestial kitchen; he held the Master’s three-carriages of playthings in low esteem and did not accord him much courtesy.

Once, when the Master visited Xuan, the heavenly food did not arrive even after noon. After the Master departed, the celestial deity descended, and Xuan interrogated him regarding the reason for the delay.
At that time, he replied, "I have just seen Mahayana bodhisattvas here, whose guard is extremely strict. Because our supernatural powers cannot enter of their own accord, it is for this reason.
When Xuán heard this, he was for the first time greatly struck with wonder and admiration.
Shi Zhicong of Xixia Monastery on Mount She in the Tang dynasty resided at Baima Monastery in Yangzhou, where he specialized in the study of the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises).

Later, he crossed the Yangtze River and stayed at Anle Monastery. Encountering the fall of the Sui dynasty, he had no means to return home and thus hid among the reeds at a river mouth, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*.
For seven days he did not feel hunger, and four tigers constantly circled around him in a docile manner. Suddenly, he saw an old man approaching in a small boat.
A man came and said, "I request that you, Master, ferry me across the river. Sengcong boarded the boat, but four tigers crouched there, refusing to leave.
The master said, "Will you not cross? The tigers then rose, and they immediately crossed together. Upon reaching the southern bank, the boat and the old man suddenly vanished.
The master took the four tigers and settled them at the west of Qixia Temple. During the Zhenguan era, at the age of ninety-nine, he passed away sitting upright; the tigers mourned him.
He roared and departed.
Shi Zhiyan of Tongxuan Temple in Suzhou during the Tang dynasty was born into the Zhu family of Wu Jun. At the age of twelve, he could recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Later, he received full ordination from Master Yan of Qinhuang Temple. Possessing a vessel of virtue and dignified deportment, he deeply guarded the roots of his precepts. During the Wude era...
After seven years, he returned to his former mountain. He constantly practiced the repentance rites of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Samantabhadra*, and others.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* more than three thousand times and lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* thirty times each. He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred and ten times. His ascetic discipline was ever more diligent;

incense would burn spontaneously without being lit, and the water in his pitcher would fill itself from emptiness. His auspicious responses were manifold. This occurred in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era.
In his later years, he manifested illness. He saw a foreign monk holding a precious vase who said, "I am Amitābha.
In the future, when you are called King of Merit-Jewels in the Pure Land, it shall be I. The Master said to his disciples, "Amitābha is Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
'King of Merit-Jewels' is the name by which he will attain Buddhahood. By speaking of the cause through the effect, he is asking, 'Shall I now return to the West?'"
He then sat cross-legged and passed away.

Shi Zhantong of Zizhou during the Tang dynasty was surnamed Chen. He left secular life at the age of eight and specialized in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*. He was particularly diligent in lecturing and teaching.
Residing at Mount Niutou, he maintained excellent deportment and observed the precepts with austere integrity. A pair of geese would often attend his sermons at the appointed time.
He lectured on the Dharma more than one hundred times. On two occasions, he emitted light. During the Zhenguan era, he manifested parinirvāṇa;
at that time, the halls and rooms of the entire monastery turned white and shook violently, subsiding only after the duration of a single meal.
Shi Zhiwei of Fahua Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Tang Dynasty was of the Jiang family of Jingyun. His lineage had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

When he was eighteen years old and about to take a wife, he encountered a foreign monk on the road who said to him, "Young man, in your previous life you were Xu Ling, the Minister of the Censorate under the Chen dynasty.

Because you listened to the Venerable Zhizhe lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, you personally made five vows: first, to maintain right mindfulness at the time of death; second, not to fall [into the lower realms]..."

[He vowed not to return] to the three realms of suffering, nor to be reborn among the three types of people; fourth, he would leave home as a youth of pure innocence; fifth, he would never fall into the ranks of worldly monks.
Today, for what reason do you wish to violate your former vow? Upon hearing this, the Master was moved to realization and no longer returned home.

He immediately went to Guoqing Temple to take Zhang’an as his teacher, where he inquired after and received the essentials of the mind. Both concentration and wisdom were awakened within him, and he immediately realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra.
In the first year of the Shangyuan era, wishing to select an auspicious site to preach the Dharma, he held his mendicant’s staff and made a vow, saying:
"Wherever this staff comes to rest, that shall be my dwelling place. The staff flew from Guoqing Temple to Mount Puyong on Cangling, a distance of some five hundred li.

Because the terrain was narrow and could not accommodate a large assembly, he cast it once more into the air until it reached Mount Xuanyuan Liandan. Thereupon, the Master halted; he cleared the land and—
He cleared thorns and cut reeds; by day he lectured and by night he practiced dhyāna. With his own hand he transcribed the scriptures, and students came from all quarters in great numbers.
He divided them into nine residential quarters, naming the other [monastery] Fa-hua (Lotus). The Master’s skeletal appearance was ancient and elegant;

whenever he ascended the seat, purple clouds would cover his head like a precious canopy. Birds and sparrows would perch beside him, becoming so tame and familiar as to be extraordinary. From Fa-hua Temple...

The Xianju Monastery was about eighty *li* away from the upper slope. The Master traveled back and forth every day; whether for meals, porridge, meditation, or lecturing, he never once failed in his duties.
All claimed that the Master possessed the supernormal power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*). In the first year of the Yonglong era, he passed away while sitting in meditation.
A wondrous fragrance did not cease for seven days. At that time, he was titled the Venerable Fahuā.
The Tang dynasty monk Shi Huida was a native of Taiyuan. He specialized in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* more than five thousand times.

Whether walking or sitting, his deportment remained dignified and the sound of his recitation never ceased. He cherished the lives of all creatures; with every step he took, he gazed straight ahead while keeping his body low.

If there were insects on the ground, he would invariably turn his body to avoid them. When someone questioned him about this, the Master said: "Whether they or I shall rise or sink is not yet determined. Perhaps they will come before me."

Having attained perfect enlightenment, how could one dare to treat him with reckless contempt? In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away while sitting in meditation; after five nights had elapsed, his countenance remained as it was at the beginning.
During the Zhenguan period, Shi Yisu of Liquan Temple in Yongzhou of the Tang dynasty recited the Lotus Sūtra several thousand times. Due to illness, he...
He told his friend, Chan Master Huikuo: "Throughout my life, I have recited the sutras with the hope that there might be some sign of efficacy.
If I have been reborn in a good realm, my tongue should remain intact; you may bury it for ten years and then exhume it. If it has decayed, you will know that my recitation was without merit.

If it remains intact, then erect a stupa for it to inspire faith and devotion in others. Having finished speaking, he passed away. Ten years later, when they opened the grave to examine it, his tongue—
The tongue remained unimpaired. Those who aspired to the Way gathered like a marketplace. The multitude erected a stupa for him on the cliffs of Gangu.
Among the various Śākyas before and after him, there were many who, by reciting the Lotus Sūtra, attained the preservation of their tongue-roots; these are not recorded in full here.
Shi Yizhong of Xiangyuan’s Yin clan was a monk at the Great Ci’en Monastery in the capital of Tang. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination.
Having heard that Dharma Master Ji had newly composed a commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), he immediately went to the lecture hall.

Within five years, he had mastered both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, as well as the five treatises beginning with the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. He subsequently authored the *Fahua jing chao* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) in twenty fascicles.

When his peers saw him, there was none who did not submit in acknowledgment. Whenever he practiced the Way, he would face the northwest, concentrating his mind in internal contemplation, vowing to behold Maitreya.
One morning at dawn, while washing and rinsing his mouth, a cloud of fragrance suddenly filled the sky.
The Master looked up, joined his palms, and said, "I am but a monk of common impurity, yet the Great Sage has deigned to come in person to guide me. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
The Tang dynasty monk Shi Farong was surnamed Wei. A native of Yanling in Runzhou, he entered Mount Mao at the age of nineteen to rely upon Dharma Master Jing.

For twenty years, he applied himself with single-minded diligence and without slackening. Later, at the northern cliff of Youqi Temple on Mount Niutou, he built a separate thatched hut and made meditation and recitation his primary practice.
The mountain had long been infested with tigers, such that even woodcutters and foragers had ceased their tracks; yet after the Master entered there, they passed to and fro once more.
There was no obstruction. Furthermore, a herd of deer would circle his room and listen while remaining crouched.

During the Zhenguan era, while he was lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* beneath a cliff, white snow filled the steps; within the frozen ice, two stalks of flowers were seen, shaped like lotuses and brilliantly golden in color.
They vanished after seven days.
The monk Fache of Pu Prefecture during the Tang Dynasty was a native of Jiangzhou. From his youth, he applied himself with diligent austerity and mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

He constantly used this sutra to guide and transform all beings. In the district there was a solitary mountain, upon which the Master settled to establish his practice and founded an āraṇya (hermitage).

The site was originally high and precipitous, and it lacked a source of water. After the Master had cultivated the Way for many years, one day clear spring water gushed forth. The Regional Inspector Fang Ren—
Yù applied for a plaque for the temple’s name, which was accordingly given as "Xianquan" (Sinking Spring). Once, while traveling on the road, he encountered a leper;

he led him into the mountains, dug a cave for him, provided him with food, and had him recite the *Lotus Sūtra*. The leper was originally illiterate and moreover dull-witted, yet [Yù] taught him every sentence without ever growing weary.
By the time they reached the sixth fascicle, the leper’s disease gradually began to subside. When the scripture was completed, [the leper] was fully healed.
His eyebrows and beard grew back, and his skin was restored as it had been before.
Shi Fada of Nanhua Temple in Shaoyang Prefecture, Tang China, was a native of Hongzhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and spent his life reciting the Lotus Sūtra.
Later, he went to Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Regarding this sutra you recite, what do you take as its essential principle?

The Master replied, "I merely recite it according to the text; how could I know its fundamental purport? The Patriarch ordered him to take the sutra and recite it aloud. When the Master reached the *Parable Chapter*, the Patriarch said, "Stop!
This sutra takes the appearance of the world through causes and conditions as its essence. He continued, "The sutra says: 'For the sake of one great matter...'"
For this reason, he has appeared in the world for one great matter: the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

If you can be free from appearances while within appearances, and free from emptiness while within emptiness, and in a single thought-moment your mind opens, this is called opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
You should believe this: the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is none other than your own mind; there is nothing else. Do not seek it outwardly; it is no different from the Buddha. Thus he spoke.

The verse says: "When the mind is deluded, it is turned by the Lotus Sūtra; when the mind is awakened, it turns the Lotus Sūtra. If one recites the sūtra for a long time without clarity, one becomes an enemy to its meaning.
Without thoughts, every thought is correct; with thoughts, every thought becomes perverse. When neither existence nor non-existence is reckoned, one forever drives the white ox-cart.
Upon hearing this, the Master could not help but weep with grief, and he also praised him in verse: "I have recited three thousand fascicles of sūtras at Caoqi—"
Upon hearing a single phrase that caused him to forget [all else], he suddenly attained enlightenment to the profound essence.
During the Kaiyuan era, the Tang dynasty monk Faxuan constructed a hermitage at the eastern foot of Mount Tiantong to reside there.

Later, he moved to the Multistoried Stupa (Duobao Ta) at the southwestern corner of the mountain. There he recited the Lotus Sūtra daily, moving the deity Tiantong to ascend and descend upon the clouds.

He brought food in his hands to offer as alms. When night fell, he would circumambulate the stupa and practice walking meditation. People saw from afar that the Master’s body was equal in height to the *cakra* (spire) of the stupa;
at that time, he was called Chan Master Taibai.
Śramaṇa Wúwèi of Shèngshàn Monastery in the Capital of the Tang Dynasty was originally from Central India; his Sanskrit name was Śubhakarasiṃha.
He possessed innate spiritual endowments from birth and renounced the throne at the age of thirteen to enter the monastic life. His virtue and reputation were preeminent throughout India.

Traveling south to the coastal regions, he encountered an exceptionally sublime monastery where he attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Wherever he went to preach the Dharma, there were always many miraculous signs.
Later, he traveled to various countries aboard a merchant vessel, secretly practicing meditation and recitation. Light radiated from his mouth. At that time, Central India suffered a great drought;
the Master prayed for it in secret, and suddenly Avalokiteśvara appeared within the solar disc, holding a *kamaṇḍalu* in his hand and pouring water onto the ground.

The multitude were filled with joy and gratitude, experiencing something they had never known before. When he was about to travel to China, he loaded his scriptures upon a camel, but the camel sank into the earth.
At the river, the Master also entered after him and stayed in the dragon palace for three nights, where he expounded the essentials of the Dharma.

Upon his departure, not a single character of the Sanskrit manuscripts he carried was wet. In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, he arrived in Chang’an and, by imperial decree, resided at Ximing Temple, where he translated scriptures such as the *Gaganagañja* and the *Mahāvairocana*.
Once, during a severe drought, the Emperor sent him to pray for rain; the Master filled a vessel with...
The water in the bowl—its Sanskrit name being *śarāva*—was several hundred [in measure]. In a brief moment, an object like a dragon appeared, its head rearing above the surface of the water.

After a short while, white vapor rose from the bowl like a bolt of silk, soaring upward into the void. Wind and thunder darkened the sky until it grew pitch black, and a great rain poured down as if from a cask.
Furthermore, once during a prolonged period of torrential rain, the Master molded five clay female figures and cast incantations in Sanskrit over them; immediately, the rain cleared.
Shi Xuanglang of Qingtai Temple in Dongyang, Tang China, was surnamed Fu and was the sixth-generation descendant of the Great Being of Shuanglin during the Liang dynasty.
He left home to become a monk in his youth and received full ordination upon reaching the age of twenty.

Hearing that the Tiantai school was flourishing in the propagation of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), he traveled to Tianguan Temple in Dongyang to pay respects to Dharma Master Huikai and practice the Lotus Samādhi (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*). Disenchanted with the mundane world, his aspirations were set upon dwelling in mountain forests and valleys.
Practicing the eighteen kinds of twelve dhūta ascetic practices, he secluded himself in a rock cave at Left Creek for over forty years.
Dwelling peacefully in a single room, he considered the Dharma-realm to be vast enough for him alone. He once painted images of Avalokiteśvara and Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja on the wall of the hall;

as he burned incense and concentrated his mind, he was moved by a divine light of five colors that illuminated the entire room. Both monastics and laypeople beheld it together and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Heaven...
He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Baoyu era. He was then titled the Venerable Zuoxi.
Shi Zhanran of Jingxi, surnamed Qi, of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai during the Tang dynasty, was twenty years old when he received the scriptures from Master Lang of Zuoxi.
The Master was greatly amazed and marveled at him. Once, he dreamed that he was wearing monastic robes and, supported by two wheels, was traveling across a great river.
Zuoxi said, "Alas! You shall employ the two dharmas of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to ferry sentient beings across the abyss of birth and death.
He then bestowed upon him the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* teachings he had inherited. In the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era, he first discarded his Confucian robes and entered the monastic order.

He went to Kāiyuán Monastery in Wú to propagate the sublime Dharma, subsequently composing commentaries on the transmitted texts totaling several hundred thousand words, thereby greatly propagating the One [Vehicle].

Regarding the teaching of the "Three Contemplations of the Mind," [Amoghavajra] was constantly accompanied by forty renowned monks from the Yangtze and Huai River regions as they together paid homage at Mount Wutai.

Master Qingliang Guanding led a retinue of over a thousand followers to welcome and escort them, and everyone at that time offered words of praise. Among them was Hanguang, a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra, who said to his master:
"Recently, while traveling through India with Amoghavajra, I encountered a Brahman monk who said: 'I have heard that in the Great Tang there is...'"

"The Tiantai school of teachings can distinguish between the partial and the perfect, discern the heterodox and the orthodox, and clarify *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Could it be translated to this land?

When the Master heard this, he sighed and said, "It may be said that the Dharma has been lost in the Middle Kingdom; we sought it in all four directions, and only late did it return to the Tiantai peaks.
In the second month of the second year of the Jianzhong era, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Now, a single thought devoid of marks is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*). There is no dharma..."
That which is incomplete is called "provisional" (jia). That which is neither identical nor different is called "the Middle" (zhong). In the state of ordinary beings, these are the three causes;
in the state of the sages, they are the three virtues. Self-benefit and benefiting others are found herein alone. Having finished speaking, he leaned back against his armrest and passed away.
His works, including the *Fahua shiqian*, *Shu*, and *Ji*, are widely circulated in the world.
Shi Shen’ung of Dali Temple in Yuezhou during the Tang dynasty was of the Cai clan from Zhuji.

He entered the path at the age of twelve and relied upon Chan Master Lang of Zuoxi to study the Tiantai *Zhi-guan* and the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuanzan*. After five summer retreats, he expounded these teachings, and scholars followed him like clouds throughout the Wu and Kuai regions.
During the Tianbao era, he traveled to Chang’an and resided at An Guo Temple; later, he returned eastward and passed through Xianghan. Therein...
Wei Zichun, the Director of the Court of Imperial Secretaries, was a man of vast learning and firm spirit; when he debated with the Master, he was ultimately humbled and won over.
Yuan Xian, the Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, sighed in admiration, saying, "The Master may truly be called a *maṇi* jewel beyond the mundane world, and a lion among debaters.
Those of his time considered him a master of eloquence.
Shi Daoxian of Fulong Mountain during the Tang dynasty had extensively surveyed the works of a hundred schools and was particularly refined in his mastery of the Lotus Sūtra.

During the Dali era, he entered the capital to propagate the teachings and produced numerous writings. He was able to travel back and forth through the void, leading contemporaries to say that he possessed the realization of supernatural powers (*ṛddhipāda*).
Shi Daozun of Zhihe Mountain in Suzhou during the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Wuxing. He studied under Zuo Xi, training in the Tiantai *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation).
Desiring to transcribe many copies of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he established a scripture hall at Zhihe and selected fourteen śramaṇas of refined conduct to constantly recite the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Using candles to extend the daylight, they propagated the Mahāyāna. By imperial decree, he was appointed as a Dharma Master.

At the Huadong Monastery, the Master cast an image of Vairocana and a stupa for Prabhūtaratna Buddha. He cultivated the practices for rebirth in the Pure Land and fashioned an image of Amitābha Buddha.
On ordinary days, he lectured on the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) without a single day of idleness throughout the year.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, while practicing the *Lotus Samādhi* at the Lingyan Monastery, he suddenly beheld a great radiance shining upward.
The Master was in the midst of light. On another day, he asked Master Yan of Jingxi: "Yan replied, 'The radiance of wisdom flows forth from the mind;

it is intended to manifest the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-dhātu). Furthermore, while entering the Dharma Flower (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) ritual arena, he beheld this body sitting in mid-air and knew it to be a sign of the purification of defilements.
In the first year of the Xingyuan era, he passed away while seated. His disciple Linghan [recorded this]."
Equaling the [building of] trees and stupas:
Shi Shenyu of Longxi, a monk of Mount Shiyi in Runzhou during the Tang dynasty, suffered from a malignant disease since childhood. During the Kaiyuan era...

Before an image of Bodhi, he burned off a finger in repentance, praying for the dispersal of his past karma. He was moved by a wondrous light like that of the moon, which illuminated the azure heavens;

his ailment was instantly cured. In the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he left the household life and received full ordination. Whenever he entered the Dharma Flower (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) ritual arena, he would [perform his devotions].
For ninety days he performed prostrations and recitations, and the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha manifested before him. He then said to his disciples: "How can the clouds and mist harm the sun?
The wind moves through space yet remains unmoving. If one truly understands that all is illusory, who is not of the nature [of reality]?

Thereupon, he established a dwelling on the east side of Laolao Mountain and constantly practiced meditative concentration. One night, a mountain deity appeared in person and declared himself to be the former [deity] of the Sui dynasty.

The Marquis Xincheng had long presided over the Southern Ridge. He now wished to offer this land forever for the practice of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight.
Ten years later, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). Upon cremation, relics (*śarīra*) were obtained in profusion, shining brightly and numbering many.
Śramaṇa Zhilin of Dà'ān Guó Temple in the capital of the Táng dynasty was surnamed Fàn. A native of Yǎn, his mother was of the Wáng clan and did not believe in the Triple Gem.

Zhilin fled to the Eastern Capital and took ordination as a Vinaya Master under the guidance of Guǎngshòu Temple. In the tenth year of the Kāiyuán era, longing for his parents, he returned home to visit them.
Three years had already passed since his mother’s death; consequently, he went to a mountain shrine to spread out his bedding and recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, vowing to behold [her].
The Master sought the place where his mother was reborn. At night, he saw the Emperor summon him and say, "Your mother is in a prison, currently undergoing all manner of suffering.
The Master wailed with grief and prayed for her release. The Emperor said, "If you go to Mount Mao and pay homage to the Stūpa of King Aśoka, she may perhaps be saved.

The next morning, the Master arrived at the temple; weeping in lamentation, he prostrated himself until he had completed forty thousand bows. Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air calling out "Neighboring! and he beheld his mother.

In a short while, they reached the shore. One day, while he was hosting a vegetarian feast at his home, a monk arrived late and said to him, "The world is currently in turmoil;
fortunately, you have not been caught in the calamity. You will eventually encounter a time of peace and attain wealth and nobility.
Having spoken, the monk vanished. When Wenben went to the feast, he found two *śarīra* relics in his bowl. Later, he served the Tang dynasty as Grand Secretary.
Wang Yan, the Tang Dynasty Court Gentleman for the Palace Gate, was dull-witted from birth. It took him a long time before he could master the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Later, when he fell ill and passed away, he appeared in a dream to his younger brother Gu, the Governor of Xin’an, saying: "Because I recited the sutra, I have attained rebirth in the Western Paradise.
However, due to my dullness, I still remain within the womb of an iron-leafed lotus flower. I inform you all of this so that you may diligently practice the sutra."
"Take care of it; do not let it fall into neglect. Having spoken these words, they parted.
Li Guyuan of Longzhou, a native of Baxi, was a devoted believer in the Buddha-dharma. Following the instructions of Master Hang, he transcribed a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The binding and case were magnificent and well-crafted; he reverently enshrined it at his estate in Qizhou. One night, it was consumed by a wildfire.
The fire spread and the entire manor house was reduced to ashes. Dao-gui ordered the ashes to be cleared away so that he might retrieve the golden and copper sutra scrolls;

however, while the outer cases were already charred to dust, the sutras themselves remained perfectly intact, their yellowed lacquer colors unchanged. This occurred in the fifth year of the Zhenguan era.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, Dong Xiong of Henan served as the Vice Director of the Court of Judicial Review (Dali Cheng).

On account of the matter involving Li Xianton, the Emperor became enraged and dispatched the Palace Attendant Wei Cong to interrogate him with extreme urgency. Dozens of officials, including Li Jingxuan of the Court of Judicial Review and Wang Xin the Rectifier (Sizhi), were all imprisoned together with him.
Dong Xiong focused his mind exclusively on the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, reciting it thirty times daily, and likewise at night.
He did not cease. Suddenly, his shackles and locks fell away of their own accord. Startled, he informed the guards. That night, the Censor-in-Chief Zhang Shouyi was on duty and stayed overnight;
he personally inspected the matter and found it most extraordinary. He re-locked them and sealed them strictly before departing. Sengxiong continued reciting the sutras.

At the fifth watch, the locks again fell away with a sound, yet the seal and inscription remained as they were. Those within and without the Imperial Chancellery who heard of this marveled at the event.

Peace. In Shi Village, south of Fushui in Chang’an County of the Tang Dynasty, there was a man named Shi Asui who had recited the Lotus Sūtra throughout his life. His fellow prisoners were all granted amnesty together with him.

He was named Chong and served as a clerk. Whether traveling to or returning from his duties, he always walked on foot and never rode a horse; this was likely in accordance with the sutras, out of compassion for all living beings.
At the time of his death, a rare fragrance filled the air, and everyone marveled at it. Ten years later, his wife passed away; they opened the grave and interred her together with him.
Li Shanlong, a native of Fengyi and a Right Cavalry Guard of the Tang dynasty, had his tongue-root severed. During the Wude era, he died suddenly; however, his heart remained warm.
After seven days, he revived and recounted that he had arrived at an official precinct where thousands of prisoners were all shackled and standing facing north.
The King asked, "What meritorious deeds did Shanlong perform throughout his life? Shanlong replied, "When my fellow villagers established a religious assembly, I constantly gave them material goods.
The King asked again, "What other virtuous practices did you perform? Shanlong said, "I recited two fascicles of the *Lotus Sūtra* every day. The King rose and said, "Excellent!
You may ascend the steps and take the high seat in the northeast to recite it. Shanlong immediately raised his voice and began the scripture.
He said, "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Chapter One: The Introduction. The King said, "Stop! Your recitation of the sutra is not merely for your own benefit;
it has caused all the prisoners in this courtyard to hear the Dharma and attain liberation. Excellent! Thereupon, the prisoners suddenly vanished.
The King ordered the dragon to be released and returned. As he traveled east, he saw an iron city, vast and immense. An official said, "This is the Great Hell."

There were partitions; each person, according to their original karma, went to the hells to undergo punishment. When Shanlong heard this, he was filled with grief and fear, and calling out "Namo Buddha," he requested the officials to let him out.
Suddenly, he saw people sitting and lying down beside him. Shanlong questioned them, and they replied, "These are the retributions for our sins."
He was about to enter the cauldron of boiling water when he heard a worthy person call out, "Namo Buddha. Consequently, all the sinners were granted a temporary respite for one day.
Chang'an's Tang official Gao Biao-ren’s grandson constantly recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. In the first month of the third year of the Longshuo era, while riding his horse—
As he was exiting through the Shunyi Gate, two riders pursued him, claiming they were messengers from the underworld sent specifically to track him down.
In great terror, Gao fled westward, intending to seek refuge at Puguang Temple; however, the ghosts hurried forward to block the gate and would not let him enter.
He then fled further west, intending to enter Kaishan Temple, but the ghosts again blocked his path. They finally rode together into Liquan Ward, with one rider leading the way before Gao.

He struck him down with his fist. Thereafter, the ghost grew enraged; from afar, he pulled Gao’s hair and hurled him down from his horse. His family carried him back home, and he did not regain consciousness until evening.
He said that he had clearly seen the King of the Netherworld, who asked, "Why did you steal the monks' fruit and further speak ill of the Triple Gem?
Gao prostrated himself and admitted his guilt, not daring to say anything more. The King said, "For the crime of stealing fruit, you ought to swallow four hundred iron pellets."

There were fifty pellets. It took four years for him to consume them all, at which point the retribution for his slander was exhausted. His tongue was then ploughed; he was released and returned home.
Upon speaking, his voice would suddenly fail, and his mouth appeared as if it had swallowed something. His entire body broke out in red blisters. Only after several days did he regain consciousness.

Thus it continued for four years until the retribution for swallowing the pellets was exhausted. Suddenly, his breath ceased again, and his spirit arrived before the King of Hell. The King commanded the ghost-wardens to pull out his tongue and plough it.

The ghost took up a chisel and gouge, both sharper than usual, yet in the end he could not reach [the tongue]. The King then examined the records and learned that it was due to the power of [the monk] having previously read the *Lotus Sūtra*;
thus his tongue could not be pulled out, and he was pardoned and released.
Thereafter, he constantly practiced the Five Repentances at Huadu Monastery to expiate his prior transgressions.
Pān Guǒ, a man from the capital of the Tang dynasty, was in his early twenties. He served as a minor official in charge of waterworks for Fùpíng County.
Upon returning home, he went out into the countryside with several youths and saw a sheep grazing on grass. Guǒ and the youths seized it and brought it back.
While on the road, the sheep bleated and cried out. Fearing that its master might hear it, he pulled out its tongue and killed it for food.
