He took this as his name. Upon returning south to Shaolin, he paid homage to the image of the First Patriarch. While traveling on the road through Dong'e, he attained sudden and complete enlightenment.
He then composed a verse which said: "Birth and death are like day and night; the water flows and the flowers fall. Today I have finally realized that my nostrils point downward.
Thereupon, he went to Beitaishan and dwelt in the most secluded and precipitous part of Longmen. In a few dilapidated rafters, he was occasionally seen.

Amidst ten thousand mountains of ice and snow, his body and mind were refreshed and serene. The mountain stream surged and roared like thunder, yet when not a single thought arose, all the clamor became as silent.

The Master made a vow to draw blood and gild the characters to transcribe one copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, thereby establishing a karmic connection with the *Prajñāpāramitā* and repaying his boundless debt of gratitude to his parents.
At that time, he frequently experienced extraordinary dreams, in which he beheld the Venerable Maitreya within a vast and expansive pavilion, expounding the wondrous Dharma for him.

Dharma. Furthermore, he dreamed that he entered a Vajra Cave and saw the Great Master Qingliang reclining upon a great jeweled couch, revealing the contemplation of the perfectly interfused realm (*yuanrong guanjing*).

From that time on, his long-standing karmic obstructions were cleared away like melting ice. In the year Yiwu of the Wanli era, due to being implicated in the matter of escorting the Tripitaka, he was exiled to Leizhou.
Upon reaching Jinling, he met Chan Master Daguan; as they parted ways, [Daguan] took him by the arm and said, "I have long heard that you, Master, are difficult to encounter. Regarding the Buddha...
Previously, he had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* one hundred times to repent for his past transgressions, saying, "My mind is my teacher’s tongue. The Master agreed.
Later, when he reached the region beyond the passes, he constructed a meditation hall amidst the fortifications and gathered the assembly to chant and study, thereby fulfilling his former vow.

He continued lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* for one full cycle. Upon reaching the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa," he attained profound awakening to the Buddha’s intent. In the year Wu-wu (1658), he settled permanently at Fayun Temple on Mount Wuyulu in Mount Lu.
Emulating Master Huiyuan, he measured time by burning incense in place of water clocks during the six periods of the day, devoting himself single-mindedly to the practice of pure karma.
The Master once used the categories of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" to interpret the entire sutra, producing the *Fahua Tongyi* (General Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) in seven fascicles.

The monk Hong'en of Jinling Daba'en Temple was surnamed Huang and was a native of Jinling. At the age of thirteen, while listening to a lecture on the *Lotus Sutra*, he reached the passage, "The three realms are without peace;
they are like a burning house," and attained a sudden and profound realization. He then requested his father’s permission to leave the household life. Together with...
Chan Master Deqing of Hanshan, together with his teacher Wuji Heshang, traveled to Mount Song and Mount Shao. Upon reaching Mount Funiu, they spent the winter retreat there before returning.

He traveled to Mount Wutai once more, where he stood firm, taking full responsibility for the Dharma. During the Wanli era, he occupied the lion throne and lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, with ten thousand fingers circling him daily.
He focused exclusively on the root text to directly explore the Buddha’s intent; wherever the single rain fell, the three types of grass flourished.
The two trees were both moistened by its flow; those who heard of it marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

He preached the Dharma for nearly thirty years, and whenever he rose from his seat, he would immediately engage in meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*). Once, while dwelling in a thatched hut to practice tranquility amidst Mount Changxing, he entered *samādhi* for two days, causing the surrounding woods and buildings to tremble.
Master Han recounted the master’s life in outline, composing the "Biography of the Reviver of the Dharma Path."
Shi Zhenjue, style name Baisong, was a native of Kunshan and a monk of Mount Fulong in Mingtai. His surname was Wang. His physical appearance was extraordinary and ancient;
he possessed innate spiritual insight from his youth. Later, seeking out Buddhist scriptures, he realized the impermanence of the world.

He left the household life and received full ordination, then traveled to Wuxing to pay homage to Master Yueting, where he joined the lecture series on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Upon reaching the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*), he attained immediate enlightenment.
In the *jiǎzǐ* year of the Jiajing era, the people of Tiantai invited the Master to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*.

He was initially reluctant to go, but in a dream, a deity in vermilion robes told him, "The conditions for the Master’s journey have ripened; I shall protect you as you travel. At that time, the local customs of Tiantai were beginning to follow heterodox teachings.

The Master exerted his wondrous eloquence and swept them all away, so that everyone came to know the practice of reciting the Buddha's name to seek rebirth in the Western Paradise. For twenty-six years thereafter, every year...
There was never an empty seat; those from near and far turned toward his influence. Scholars revered him as the Dharma Master Miaofeng (Wondrous Peak).

He extensively propagated the teachings and contemplations of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Miaozongchao* (Commentary on the Wondrous Pivot). All those of his time who knew of the school of the "inherently complete nature" (*xingju zong*) did so through the virtue and transformation of this master.

At the end of his life, he composed the "Three Self-Reflections" before passing away. The Master had often practiced the *Suiziyi Samādhi* (Samādhi of Following One’s Own Intent), and whenever he encountered illness...
As for his practice, his cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* was ever more rigorous. He authored the *Zhuyou Jingtu Mengtan Ji* (Record of Dream Discourses on the Pure Land).
Ming Shi Zhenqing, styled Xiangxian, was a member of the Luo clan of Xiangtan.

In his youth, he entered Mount Nanyue and received the tonsure under Master Baolin, subsequently being ordained with the full precepts. Daily he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* while concurrently practicing ascetic disciplines. At twenty-five, he crossed the sea.
He paid his respects at Putuo. While on the boat, he suddenly attained a realization. Consequently, he visited the ancient sites of Yanguan and took up residence at Juehuang Temple.

Shortly thereafter, he fell ill; in a vision, he clearly saw Lord Guan bestow upon him a divine elixir, saying: "You are a man of ultimate attainment. I request that you propagate the profound regulations to awaken the common people of this degenerate age. His illness soon healed.
Subsequently, he traveled south to Tiantai, where he practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight) with great diligence for five years. He then returned once more.
At the Southern Peak of Huading, the Great Master Yongming of the Song dynasty once practiced meditative concentration for ninety days.

The Master [Zhili] held his style in high esteem and built a hermitage upon the old site. He established a religious society and practiced the Great and Small Amitābha Repentances for three years each. He widely praised the Tiantai school and diligently expounded the Five Repentances.
One night, he dreamed of a magnificent jade palace where Amitābha and the Three Holy Ones were seated in rows; the Master then prostrated himself before them.
He saw a novice monk being given a plaque inscribed with the four characters: "Perfumed by the Fragrance of Precepts" (*Jiexiang xunxiu*).

The Master resolved to participate, forgetting all fatigue, and diligently practiced the long-term retreat three times over nine cycles of winter and summer.

Each time he obtained auspicious responses, yet he remained silent and spoke of them to no one. Later, when he ceased his formal chanting and recitation, while walking along the path by West Creek, he [shouldered...]

The monk Sengfu of Jiangyin was renowned for his lofty and profound virtue. Toward the end of the Wanli era, he frequently transcribed the Lotus Sūtra, completing it only after many years.
Upon finishing the transcription, he cast his writing brush into a pond. It happened to be the first month of winter, a time of intense cold, yet suddenly a single lotus flower emerged.
It emerged from within the ice and rose straight up, towering and solitary. The Master thereupon styled himself the "Ice Lotus Immortal" (Binglian Daoren).
Xia Xiaolian Shufang took him as his teacher and personally absorbed his extraordinary influence.

The Master performed the recitation before the altar of Wei Tian and dedicated the merit. Zhou possessed a very strong ox that suddenly died thereafter. Not long after, the spirit of the deceased attached itself to the body of a woman and called out.

The son said, "Previously, because my karmic burden of speech was heavy, I became an ox. Now, through the merit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I have already been liberated from the suffering of an ox.

If I may request Master Lang to perform rites of repentance once more, I shall then be able to take rebirth. The Master then performed the rites of repentance for him and offered the *yankou* (flaming-mouth) food.
That night, Zhou saw his mother in a vision, who thanked him, saying, "By the power of these repentance rites, I have already taken rebirth as a neighbor to the east."
The following morning, he recounted his dream to the Master. It happened that a son had been born to the Zheng family of the eastern neighbor; they looked at one another in astonishment.
When asked when this had occurred, [the Master replied], "It was just as your family’s Dharma hall was being completed. The Master had once transcribed the Lotus Sūtra using his own blood;

having finished writing its sixty thousand-odd words, they flowed forth as if through long-standing practice. In the meditation chamber where he resided, lotus flower petals and stalks were found covering the plastered walls.
All who behold these various signs and pay homage to Putuo Mountain rejoice and join their palms in praise.
It is known that Juefeng Temple on Xingbu Street in Beijing was the place where the ancient sandalwood Buddha image was enshrined and venerated.
In the final years of the temple, the abbot was the monk Jizhou. Throughout his life he had been sincere and upright, revering the Buddha with solemn devotion;

however, he was not strictly observant regarding the precept against alcohol. One day, a person wearing two-piece clothing came to inform him, saying, "I am a messenger of impermanence from the Underworld.
A certain old woman, having performed not a single good deed during her lifetime, is detained in hell and unable to escape. On every first and fifteenth day of the month..."

He had previously visited a temple to prostrate before the Buddha and brought fruit as an offering to his teacher. On account of these causes and conditions, he hoped that [the teacher] would recite the *Lotus Sūtra* for him once so that he might attain rebirth.
Zhou was skeptical and did not believe him, saying, "Since you are a ghost, it is difficult for you to reach the realm of the Buddha;
why not go pay your respects there? The ghost replied, "The City God (Dou Chenghuang) is within, and I do not dare to enter. Zhou—
Reflecting on this, I recall that at the fifth watch of the night, there was someone who wished to perform a virtuous deed; he established the position of the City God (Chenghuang) beside the hall.
Those words are indeed not false. Accordingly, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, I knelt before the Buddha and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
Upon reaching the fifth fascicle, the weather was hot and she was extremely thirsty. Unable to find tea, she saw a wine jug on a table; shaking it, she found there was still some left.
She then took a sip of the cold wine and continued kneeling before the Buddha to complete the scripture. The next day, Wuchang returned and said:
"The old woman followed the Master’s recitation of the sutra and completed four fascicles. Consequently, throughout the underworld, golden light radiated everywhere. This was precisely...

As he was about to depart from hell and take rebirth, suddenly a gust of the scent of wine rushed into the underworld; this occurred consistently from fascicle five through fascicle seven, and thus [the deceased] still could not gain liberation.
When Zhou heard of this, his hair stood on end and his skin crawled with awe. He made a vow of utmost sincerity and recited the scripture for him as a supplement.
From this point on, he strictly observed the precept against alcohol, never daring to transgress it again. Lord Tang once engraved this account upon a stone.

However, [the monk] asked, "What retribution for sin shall I receive? The boy replied, "You shall fall among the dung-worms. Having finished speaking, he vanished. The monk was greatly terrified. Later, he washed himself thoroughly according to the Dharma.

Zhiji), a member of the Zhang clan from Guangshan in Henan, read the classics at Bailudong (White Deer Grotto) upon reaching the age of twenty.
He encountered a strange monk who told him, "You are in great danger; if you can maintain the recitation of the name of the Holy One of Great Compassion, it may be resolved.

The Master vowed his heart to maintain this practice. In the Xinsi year of the Chongzhen era, the rebel Xian invaded and destroyed the county; when the slaughter reached the Master, his blade suddenly snapped of its own accord.

The rebels were astonished by this and he escaped death. Thereupon, he resolved to shave his head and become a monk. In the Jiashen year, he arrived in Jinling and followed the Venerable Meitong of Qianhua.
Having received full ordination, he saw that the region was filled with warhorses and cavalry; he therefore traveled eastward along the river until he reached Kunshan.

In a pure chamber there, he lectured on the Brahmajāla, Vajracchedikā, Śūraṅgama, and other sutras, and both monastics and laypeople took refuge in him with devotion. In the spring of the wu-zi year, the Xu family donated a villa in the western suburbs and invited the Master to reside there.
In the spring of the geng-yin year, he delivered a lecture on the Lotus Sutra; his analytical wisdom arose like clouds, and the assembly of listeners...
The daily attendance reached ten thousand. A white crane descended from the sky, circled the dharma assembly several times, and after listening to the teachings, departed with a sharp, long cry.
He then named his hermitage "Dharma Rain" (Fayu). In the year Xinmao, during a great famine in Kun County, he presided over the distribution of rice gruel.
His mental and physical strength were both exhausted, and he subsequently fell ill. On the second day of the first month of the *Renchen* year, he sat upright, recited a verse, and passed away.
During the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty, there was a monk named Yongning, with the style name Xilin, who resided as the abbot of Baoen Temple.

He kept a horse which he would ride from the temple whenever he went to the Ministry of Rites. At the time of mounting the horse, he would silently recite the *Lotus Sūtra*; by the time he dismounted at the gate of the Ministry, it was exactly finished.
The *Zong* (Essentials) is one fascicle; it is generally treated as a standard text. Opposite the gate of the temple, there was a pregnant woman who dreamed at night that this horse entered her room.
She subsequently gave birth to a son. At dawn, she went to the temple to inquire about it, and it was found that the horse had died at that very moment.

Her family later made the boy a disciple of Xilin. He was extremely dull-witted; when taught the written characters, he could not recognize even a single one, knowing them only through oral transmission.

A single scroll of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was sufficient for him to recite with fluency; his faith was such that he attained liberation upon hearing the sutra. This appears in the *Jinling Suoshi*.

Furthermore, there was a monk in Danghu who was reciting the *Lotus Sutra*. A frog heard the sound of the recitation and suddenly assumed a posture of bowing its head and kneeling with its hands clasped, maintaining this for some time.
After a short while, it sat as if in meditation; when shaken, it was found to have already died. — Recorded by Xiu Ya of the Tang Dynasty.
The Dharma Master said: "The Buddha’s intent is the marrow of the Patriarchs; my own heart is the purport of the scriptures. Close your eyes, quiet your minds, and listen closely.

In the winter of the Xinmao year, he fell into a stupor. While in this state of delirium, he heard a voice from the ulcer speaking in human speech, saying: "I am Lu Zhaorong of the Liang dynasty."
He was in the palace at Luoyang when he met his end at the hands of bandits; more than six hundred years have passed since then, yet his name still lingers in the registers of the dead.
You, who were the very one that day who took my life, have now been reborn as a man. You ought to transcribe the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and other scriptures to save yourself and me.
Wen Zhu, weeping and praying while enduring his pain, immediately began to write. At that time, he was residing in Yizhen and completed the task.
Paper and brush. He transcribed sutras such as the Lotus, the Avataṃsaka, the Vajracchedikā, and the Śūraṅgama, as well as the Water Repentance Ritual.

Every time he wrote, his pain would suddenly cease; yet once he set down the brush, the pain would return. After more than a year, when his transcription of the sutras was complete, his ailment was finally cured.

The monks of the temple provided him with a separate room to dwell in. He requested paper and brushes and wrote the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Fǎhuá Jīng*) using half-folds of silk.

Minglong De fu became the Vice Governor (Jun-cheng) of Siming. He was upright and honest and fond of the Way. At that time, there were two abbots at Putuo.

The first was named Dazhi (Great Wisdom). He was strict and rigorous in his observance of the precepts, and both monastics and laypeople looked up to him in devotion. The second was named Zhenbiao (True Manifestation).

Although he presided over a monastic community (*conglin*), he was by nature fierce and violated the precepts. In the *Renwu* year of the Wanli era, he was commissioned by the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner to investigate a matter concerning the flogging of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) for a minor offense.
Upon arriving at the mountain monastery, he issued a decree to take a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and burn it, ordering the assembly of monks to do so.
He stepped completely across them all, vowing never to commit such an offense again. Having reached the rear palace to pay his respects, he felt his two thighs become numb and weak, unable to move.
His body broke out with a strange fever, and his illness soon left him utterly exhausted and delirious. In this state of confusion, he vaguely heard an imperial edict being proclaimed:

"To serve the Way and yet destroy the Way is particularly deserving of severe punishment. However, out of consideration for the people, he shall be punished by serving as the Supervisor of Three Stone Oxen. He was subsequently appointed as a Vice Director.
I reflected that this must be the summons of the underworld officials; thus I have died and shall enter the evil realms. I did not realize that the sin of destroying a scripture was so great.
From this day forward, I vow to observe the precepts and fast for the rest of my life; I beg to resign my office immediately to enter the Way and redeem myself.
Master Dazhi also offered prayers, recited scriptures, and performed repentance rituals on my behalf. Within his meditative concentration, he beheld an Iron Encircling City.
Naked corpses lay piled up within the city, and the Prefect was among them; he alone was not naked.
The Master repented with a sincere heart, when suddenly he saw a single beam of white light descend from the sky as if someone were supporting him out and restoring him to life.

The Prefect saw the śramaṇas gathered like clouds and asked why he had burned the sutras and violated this great precept. The Prefect replied, "I recognize my transgression. I wish to repay one hundredfold for every single offense."
He first donated his stipend to provide a vegetarian feast for ten thousand monks, whereupon the assembly of śramaṇas vanished.

That evening, while it was pitch black, the governor’s servant saw two jade maidens with their hair tied in double topknots, carrying banners and canopies in their hands as they brushed past the bed; there was a sudden *huì* sound.

As the base of a banner brushed against the servant’s face, he started up in alarm and cried out loudly; the governor’s illness was immediately cured. At that time, he had not eaten nor blinked for ten days.

When Zhū Yuánzhèng of Hǎiyán was still a student, he lectured on the teachings of Confucius and Mencius; he was upright and never acted with levity.

You do not realize that my life and death have already been decisively settled. Why speak of such things again?"
When the Master was about to pass away, he took a brush and drew a line upon the desk with his hand; this signified that he had already resolved the matter of birth and death.
Those who witnessed it were all struck with awe and felt profound reverence. In the seventh month, being free from illness, he suddenly said to his son, "I have no further business here;
I may now depart. His son asked, "Where will you go? He replied, "To the West. Although his son and grandson earnestly entreated him to stay, he would not.

He granted their request. When the first day of the twelfth lunar month arrived, he manifested illness and ceased eating. His family members were in a state of panic as they prepared for his funeral affairs.
The Master said, "Do not be anxious; this is an event for the midnight of the eighth day of the twelfth month. When that time came, he sat upright, intending to pass away.

He spoke again, saying, "In my entire life, I have not failed anyone by even a hair’s breadth. This winter, the carpenter behind my house repaired a patch of ground for me at the back gate. He then covered it...
He expressed his hope to receive guests on New Year’s Day. As he was walking across the level courtyard, the old man’s gait faltered.
His refined intention had not yet been acknowledged, so [the host] took paper and composed a poem of thanks; however, he wrote one character incorrectly and attempted to erase it with his brush.

Just as he sat down calmly, he passed away. It was then the hour of the rooster’s crow. The Master had previously instructed his family that when the time of his departure arrived, they must not allow women to be present.
"Come. You may come after two or three hours have passed. When you arrive, do not weep. By the time day breaks, your kinsmen will have arrived to offer their condolences.
Once the Master has awakened again, he will open his eyes but not speak; instead, he will shake his head to have the women leave.
When they have all departed, he will close his eyes and pass away. At that time, his coming and going were as free as this. He had already requested a letter from Miaoyi An.
Mingwang Ligu (明王立轂), courtesy name Bemu (伯無), was a native of Taizhou. In his youth, he followed his father, the Grand Secretary Zhongcheng Shixing (士性), on a journey to Mount Jizu.
There, they entered through a stone wall, where they encountered Kāśyapa, who asked, "From where have you come? Wang was startled and took a sudden fright.
Kāśyapa said, "You have fallen into the burning house; practice compassion, patience, and the precepts, so that one day you may courageously withdraw from the swift current."

The body of Qiaoxia from his previous life remained as it was; in an instant, the walls closed back together just as before. From this point on, the King strictly observed the precept against killing.

In the *Wanli* era, during the *Bingwu* year, he passed the provincial examination. He dreamed that his father told him he would die five times over ten years and instructed him to cultivate virtue to avert disaster.
He then made a vow before the Three Treasures of Jiahe to observe the perpetual fast and received the four precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying at Mount Tiantai.
Later, serving as the Magistrate of Xingan County, he entered the capital for an audience in the year Wu-wu. While his boat was moored at Digang, he was summoned by the underworld at night.
The presiding official shouted with a stern voice, "Your earthly lifespan was due to end in the eighth month of the Bingchen year; that it has been extended until now..."
"This is the power of fasting and purification. Why do you abandon it? The King bowed and apologized, saying, "In my official capacity, I could not help but act thus.
The Master said, "That may be so, but what can be done when one's lifespan is exhausted? He ordered him to be driven into prison.

A subordinate official on the left side requested, "Please allow me to examine the records of his conduct after he broke his precepts. After a short while, two baskets arrived from Yi, containing a bundle of documents and another [item].
A single document was displayed; all the slips of paper, each only a few inches square, upon which he had customarily practiced his calligraphy were there as well.

Each emitted a rising vapor of various colors—blue, black, red, and white. The presiding official ordered them to be sorted and examined. First, the black and blue slips were gathered together into a heap.

Next, he examined the white cluster; the blue one gradually shrank. He then examined the red cluster; the blue one vanished, and the black one shrank to about the size of a cup, while the red vapor blazed alone and grew exceedingly intense.
The King gazed at it and saw that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Hao-sheng-pian* (Treatise on Cherishing Life), and the scrolls concerning the community granary were all present.
The custodian said, "This shows that by planting virtue, one still possesses the principle of survival. [The King] damaged...
"The five sense organs are sufficient for the preservation of one's body and life; yet he ordered his eyes to be gouged out, leaving him dim-sighted and unable to see anything.
He felt someone urging him to walk, but upon taking a single step, he woke up. When he opened his eyes, the sight of the lamps was like needles piercing him, such that he could not open them at all."
The physician administered eye-cleansing medicine. That night, it felt as though someone were once again nailing his eyes shut, causing his pain to intensify greatly.

He subsequently rejected further medical treatment and resolved to resign from his post to return to his hometown. Abandoning his household life, he cultivated pure practices and vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra one thousand times.
He also recited the *Vajra-Brahmajāla Sūtra* daily to pray for spiritual protection.

In the seventh month of the Gengshen year, while performing repentance rituals at Youxi, he dreamed one evening that the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) sprinkled nectar from a willow branch onto his eyes.

Upon waking the next morning, his vision cleared suddenly and both eyes were restored to sight. Later, he traveled to the gates of Yunqi and Boshan. Twelve years after his "rebirth," he was styled Bi.
As the Great Master stated in his *Record of Returning to Life*:
"It was clearly revealed that You Hongyuan of Suzhou had a secret affair with a neighboring girl slave and pledged their lives together; he subsequently took her as a concubine."
The wife treated her with jealousy and cruelty, employing incantations and curses to cause her to die quickly. Before long, the concubine indeed passed away.

More than a year later, the wife fell ill for a long time and called upon an old village woman to stay with her. At night, she saw the concubine, dressed in red skirts and green robes, gliding slowly before her. Pointing at the wife, the concubine scolded her, saying:
"My life was not yet fated to end, yet you used incantations and curses to cause my premature death. I have now lodged a complaint with the Office of the Mountains (Yuesi)."
"I am coming for you. Having said this, he vanished. That evening, his wife indeed passed away. Yuan felt pity for the concubine’s grievance;
however, the many vows his wife had made in her lifetime, as well as the numerous documents she had left behind, would surely become a burden to him.

Consequently, he daily recited the *Yuhuang Jing* (Scripture of the Jade Sovereign) several hundred times. He also prayed to Zhenwu, the deity he served, and consulted the Daoist Lian at Xuanmiao Guan regarding divination.
He established a ritual site for both land and water (*shuilu daochang*) to atone for his past transgressions. Later, while Huiyuan was ill, he saw himself being led away by a subordinate officer.

They arrived at a gate inscribed with the name "Yuefu" (The Office of the Mountains). A King sat upon the throne in the hall and, after shouting a question, was informed of his wife’s account regarding the matter of incantations and curses committed together with Huiyuan.

Huiyuan knelt and pleaded that it was not his own fault. The King called his attendants to press Huiyuan’s wife and concubines forward to testify. His wife’s excuses were exhausted, and the King said: "You..."
Although he did not know the details of the case, this woman’s litigations were numerous; how could they be resolved?
Yuan Yuan had not yet replied when the presiding official presented a judgment to the King, saying, "The High Truth (the Buddha) already possesses the written documents to settle this matter.

The King ordered the records to be inspected and examined them, then handed them to Yuan. Yuan was so terrified that he had no leisure to read them closely; he saw only several lines of vermilion script.
At the end of the document, the King said, "When sending official correspondence to Fengdu, one should say 'Presented' (呈). To say 'Consulted' (咨) now is an error.
Suddenly, two armored divine generals appeared in the courtyard: one was the Holy Lord Guan (Guansheng), and the other was the Heart General, King Lingguan. Lingguan looked at the King and said:
"This minor offense is not worth questioning," the King nodded in agreement. The Spirit Official kicked Yuan with his foot, saying, "Go! Yuan was thus able to leave.
After several turns along the road, he entered another office where six monks were seated within. They called out to Yuan and interrogated him. The presiding official said, "Return for now;
you shall enter the Office of the Five Pestilence Spirits. Yuan explained in detail the reason for the High Truthful One’s shame regarding his transgressions. The monks said:
"You know that while you have honored the Way, you have forgotten the Buddha; even the immediate consequences of this are no small matter.
Now that you have been granted the return to life, you ought to urgently invite six monks of long-standing seniority and high virtue to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* six times.

Only then can your transgressions be extinguished. He then ordered his release. After several days, Yuan invited the monks to recite the sūtras according to the prescribed number, which continues to this day.
Every month on the first day of the lunar cycle, he would regularly maintain his recitation of scriptures and perform repentance rites; though extremely busy, he never neglected them.

Ming Ge Wan, whose courtesy name was Shiping, was a native of Kunshan. He surrendered himself to the study of the Way and, with his doors closed, researched the Buddhist canon (*Zhufun*) tirelessly for many years.

He placed particular devotion in the *Lotus Sūtra*, which he used as his daily practice. He reflected that time flows like a fleeting lightning bolt and that the wondrous Dharma is difficult to encounter.
I have heard that to repay the Buddha’s kindness, the propagation of the sutras is the essential task.

Consequently, I have compiled the *Gantong lu* (Records of Resonance and Response) in four volumes, drawing upon the deeds of former sages and ancient virtuous masters from the Jin and Song dynasties down through the Yuan and Ming. At the end of each volume, I have appended a treatise. Although several years have passed, the work remains unfinished.

In the autumn of the Xinmao year, I had been afflicted by physical decline and illness for a full year. By the winter of the Renchen year, I repeatedly experienced extraordinary dreams over several consecutive nights, in which I saw divine beings urging me to carve this compilation.
Thereupon, I exerted all my strength to assemble the craftsmen, and when the transcription was completed, my illness soon subsided.
In the Ming dynasty, there was a man from Wumen named Chen Jisheng, styled Huangshi. He was the eldest son of the Duke Wen Zhuang.

By nature, he practiced virtuous deeds with diligence; regarding all noble words and exemplary conduct of the past and present, he personally compiled and recorded them until they nearly filled his library.

He was particularly fond of the Buddhist scriptures and frequently formed a *lotus society* to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, persevering without weariness for a long time. One night, he suddenly dreamed of an elderly man with a wind-swept appearance...
The deity was ancient and extraordinary. In his hand he held a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* written in gold characters, along with accounts of karmic causes and effects which he transmitted to me.

Chenzi (the Master Chen) leapt for joy, prostrated himself, and accepted them. At dawn, the *Fahua Gantong Lu* (Record of Miraculous Responses to the Lotus Sutra), carved by the Ge family of Lucheng, was indeed found and circulated through the Yuanyao Hall of Master Chen.
Furthermore, another friend brought a complete set of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* written in gold on clay.
The substance [of this matter] is the same as the events of that day. Not long after, while traveling, he again encountered a gilded *Lotus Sūtra* written by Li Zhengqing of Xin’an;
he purchased it and brought it back for veneration, thereby completing the pair. Its majesty was sublime and wondrous, such that onlookers marveled at its rarity.
Only then did he believe that what is moved by profound sincerity and the karmic conditions of Buddhist affairs are indeed inconceivable in this way. — Recorded by Chen.

Among the works authored by him, the *Gongzhi lu* (Record of Shared Knowledge), the *Tongshan hui quanlu* (Complete Record of the Assembly for the Cultivation of Goodness), and the *Xianglin guangshu* (Extensive Writings of Xianglin) have been compiled and circulated in the world.
Regarding Lady Yan, the mother of Minister Tan Zhenmo of the Ming dynasty: she maintained her household and educated her son with equal adherence to the laws and standards of propriety. Although...

Her husband was noble, yet she lived as a commoner in simple clothing and plain food, possessing profound faith in the Buddha-dharma. She held the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in especially high esteem, reciting them morning and evening.

In her later years, she maintained the empowerment of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, reading one fascicle daily. Furthermore, she was able to explain the great principles of the scriptures for her son and daughter-in-law.
In the *Ren-shen* year of the Chongzhen era, she manifested illness; rising to bathe and change her robes, she prostrated before the Buddha and said: "I, one..."

He conceived a deep reverence for the Buddha. Because he possessed the karmic affinity for the Buddha, his physical remains were not subject to decay. He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture with palms joined.
At that time, it was the seventh day of the hot season, yet his countenance bore a smile as if alive, and a fragrant scent wafted forth from time to time.
Not a single fly hovered near the funeral site; all who saw this could not help but marvel at it in wonder.
